lead: Paul sets out again, now with Silas and a young man from Lystra named Timothy. The Holy Spirit closes one road after another, until a vision in the night opens the way: a man of Macedonia pleading, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” The Gospel crosses into Europe in answer to a cry for help. In the Gospel Jesus warns his friends that the world which hated him will hate them too. Psalm 100 calls all the earth to make a joyful noise to the Lord: the mission, its cost and its joy belong together.

r.h: Come over to Macedonia
set: This is the beginning of what is often called Paul’s second missionary journey. After the meeting in Jerusalem (Acts 15), Paul and Barnabas parted company over John Mark, and Paul chose Silas instead (15:36–41). Now he revisits the churches of the first journey and finds at Lystra a disciple named Timothy, whose mother was a Jewish believer and whose father was Greek. Second Timothy 1:5 names his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, women of sincere faith.

Background. “Asia” here is not the continent but the Roman province of Asia, in the west of present-day Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city. Bithynia lay to the north, along the Black Sea. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, not far from ancient Troy. Across the sea lay Macedonia, the Roman province in northern Greece, with the cities of Philippi and Thessalonica.
str: vv. 1–3: Timothy joins Paul, and Paul has him circumcised.
vv. 4–5: the decisions of Jerusalem are delivered; the churches grow.
vv. 6–8: the Spirit closes the way into Asia and Bithynia; they come down to Troas.
vv. 9–10: the vision of the man of Macedonia, and the first “we”.
kw: Only here in the New Testament (v. 7). In v. 6 Luke says “the Holy Spirit”, in v. 7 “the Spirit of Jesus”: the same Spirit, whom the Risen Lord pours out and through whom he still leads his Church.
Luke uses this word for the visions that guide the Church at turning points: to Ananias (9:10), to Cornelius (10:3) and to Peter (10:17). God speaks when the road is unclear.
Literally to put things together (v. 10). The companions weigh the closed doors and the vision together and come to a decision. God’s guidance and careful human thought work side by side.
vv: the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer; but his father was a Greek.
Timothy grew up between two worlds. Many scholars think that the son of a Jewish mother would have been regarded as a Jew, which helps to explain the next verse.
he took him and had him circumcised because of the Jews who were in those places,

This can surprise us, since Paul refused to have the Gentile Titus circumcised (Galatians 2:3). But Timothy was counted as Jewish, and Paul did not want his companion to be a stumbling block in the synagogues where they would preach. As he says himself, to the Jews he became as a Jew (1 Corinthians 9:20).
having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.

Luke does not say how: perhaps through a prophet, through circumstances, or through an inner conviction. The mission is not Paul’s own plan. A closed door is also guidance. Paul will preach in Asia later, for more than two years at Ephesus (19:8–10).
“Come over to Macedonia and help us.”
The first call to bring the Gospel into Europe comes as a plea for help. The man does not ask for new ideas; he asks for help. The Gospel is the help people most need, even when they cannot name it.
we immediately tried to cross over to Macedonia,

Here, without any explanation, the story changes from “they” to “we”. This is the first of the “we” passages of Acts (16:10–17, and later in chapters 20–21 and 27–28). Ancient tradition took them as the voice of Luke himself, Paul’s companion. Scholars still discuss them, but that remains the simplest reading.
ch: Pope St Paul VI wrote in Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) that the Church exists in order to evangelise (n. 14). The cry of the man of Macedonia is that need spoken aloud. The Catechism calls the Holy Spirit the principal agent of the whole of the Church’s mission, the one who leads her on her missionary paths (CCC 852). Today’s reading shows this in practice: the apostles plan, the Spirit redirects, and the Church goes where she is needed.

r.h: It hated me before it hated you
set: We are still at the Last Supper. Jesus has just called the disciples his friends and given them the commandment to love one another (15:12–17). Now he turns to the other side: the hatred of the world. Love within the community and hostility from outside are spoken of in the same breath.

In John, “the world” has more than one sense. God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (3:16). Here the world means humanity as it closes itself against God. The disciples are not taken out of the world; they are sent into it (17:15, 18).
str: v. 18: the world hated me first.
v. 19: chosen out of the world.
v. 20: the servant and the master.
v. 21: on account of my name.
kw: Here not the earth, nor people as such, but human life arranged without God and against him.

In the Bible “to hate” can mean to reject, to refuse to belong with. Jesus does not ask his disciples to hate in return; in the same discourse he prays for those who will believe through their word (17:20).
“I have chosen you out of the world” (v. 19) uses the same verb as “You did not choose me but I chose you” (15:16). The disciple’s identity rests on Christ’s choice, not on the world’s approval.
vv: If the world hates you, be aware that it hated me before it hated you.
Here too Jesus goes ahead of his disciples. When they suffer for him, they walk where he has already walked.
If you belonged to the world, the world would love you as its own.
A disciple who is never opposed may ask whether he has simply blended in. This is not a call to look for conflict, only to belong first to Christ.
Remember the word that I said to you, ‘Servants are not greater than their master.’
He said it after washing their feet (13:16). There it meant that they must serve as he served; here it means that they will be treated as he was treated. Both belong to being a disciple.
ch: The Church has always read these words in the light of her martyrs. St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to death in Rome, wrote that Christianity shows its greatness when it is hated by the world (in substance). The Second Vatican Council teaches that all must be ready to confess Christ before others and to follow him along the way of the cross amid the persecutions which the Church never lacks (Lumen Gentium 42, in substance). Christians in many lands suffer today for the name of Christ; the Church prays for them, and for those who wrong them.

qa: Should a Christian expect to be hated?

Not to look for it, and not to be surprised by it. Jesus speaks of hatred “on account of my name” (v. 21), not hatred we earn by harshness or pride. St Peter makes the same distinction: no one should suffer as a wrongdoer, but whoever suffers as a Christian should not be ashamed (1 Peter 4:15–16). The Christian answer to hostility is the love Jesus has just commanded, and prayer for those who persecute (Matthew 5:44).
rite: 1 May is also the optional memorial of St Joseph the Worker, instituted by Pope Pius XII in 1955; where it is kept, its own readings may be used. The carpenter of Nazareth and Paul the tentmaker (Acts 18:3) remind us that ordinary work, done with love, belongs to God’s plan.
study: When has a closed door in my life turned out to be God’s guidance?
Who around me is saying, in words or without words, “Come over and help us”?

lead: On the Sixth Sunday of Easter one word runs through all three readings: love. In the house of Cornelius, Peter learns that God shows no partiality, and the Holy Spirit falls on Gentiles before anyone has baptised them. John’s letter gives the shortest description of God in the Bible: God is love. In the Gospel Jesus shows how far that love goes: to laying down one’s life for one’s friends.

The order matters. Love begins with God, not with us (1 John 4:10). It flows from the Father to the Son, from the Son to the disciples (John 15:9), and from them outward, even to a Roman officer’s household in Caesarea. Psalm 98 sings that the Lord has made known his victory in the sight of the nations; Acts shows it happening.

r.h: God shows no partiality
set: Cornelius was a centurion of the Italian Cohort at Caesarea, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously and prayed constantly (10:1–2). An angel told him to send for Peter at Joppa. Meanwhile Peter, praying on a rooftop, saw a sheet let down from heaven full of creatures the Law counted unclean, and heard a voice telling him not to call profane what God has made clean (10:15). Then the messengers of Cornelius arrived at the door.

Background. Jewish law and custom kept a careful separation from Gentile homes and tables, as Peter himself says (10:28). It was meant to guard Israel’s holiness as God’s own people. Now Peter learns that God is also calling the Gentiles. The reading leaves out Peter’s summary of the Gospel (vv. 36–43), one of the great sermons of Acts, and moves to the moment when the Spirit interrupts him.
str: vv. 25–26: Cornelius falls at Peter’s feet; Peter raises him up.
vv. 34–35: God shows no partiality.
vv. 44–46: the Spirit falls on the Gentiles, and they speak in tongues and praise God.
vv. 47–48: Peter orders them to be baptised.

¶ Luke tells this story three times: in full in chapter 10, again in Peter’s report (11:1–18), and briefly at the meeting in Jerusalem (15:7–9). Repetition is his way of saying: this is a turning point.
kw: Literally one who “receives the face”, who judges by appearance, rank or race (v. 34). The Old Testament already says that God is not partial (Deuteronomy 10:17). Peter now sees what this means for the nations.
“The gift of the Holy Spirit” (v. 45) is the same phrase Peter used at Pentecost (2:38). The Gentiles receive the very same gift, not a lesser one, as Peter later insists (11:17).

The verb of Joel’s prophecy quoted at Pentecost: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (2:17). Here “all flesh” begins to include the Gentiles. The scene is often called the Pentecost of the Gentiles.
vv: But Peter made him get up, saying, “Stand up; I am only a mortal.”
Cornelius meant deep reverence, but Peter will not accept what belongs to God alone. The first of the apostles begins by lifting a man to his feet.
I truly understand that God shows no partiality,
Peter speaks as one still learning. Even the first of the apostles had to be taught by the Spirit, through a vision and through the faith of a Gentile.
but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

This does not mean that Christ is unnecessary: Peter at once goes on to preach Christ, and the passage ends in baptism. It means that God was already at work in Cornelius before Peter arrived, preparing him for the Gospel.
While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word.
God does not wait for Peter to finish. Elsewhere in Acts the Spirit comes with or after baptism (2:38; 8:14–17). Here he comes first, so that no one can doubt that God has accepted these Gentiles.
“Can anyone withhold the water for baptizing these people who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?”
The Spirit’s coming does not make baptism unnecessary; it is the reason Peter cannot refuse it. The gift within is joined to the sacrament of the Church.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its chapter on the People of God with v. 35: at all times and in every nation, anyone who fears God and does what is right is acceptable to him; yet God willed to make people holy and to save them not as individuals without any bond between them, but by making them into a single people (Lumen Gentium 9, in substance). That is the whole movement of this chapter of Acts: God at work in Cornelius, and then Cornelius brought into the one Church through baptism. The Council also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, yet seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try to do his will, can attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16).

r.h: God is love
set: John has just told his readers to test the spirits, because not every spirit is from God (4:1–6). Now he turns to the sign that does not deceive: love. This passage is the heart of the letter, and the words “God is love” return a few verses later (4:16).

Ancient tradition ascribes the letter to the apostle John. The letter does not name its writer, and many scholars think it comes from a disciple within the circle of John. It was written for communities wounded by division, near the end of the first century.
str: v. 7: let us love one another, because love is from God.
v. 8: whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love.
v. 9: how God’s love was revealed: he sent his only Son.
v. 10: what love is: not our love for God, but his love for us.
kw: A word rare in earlier Greek writing, which the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament made their own for the love that gives itself. In English, “love”, “loves” and “loved” occur nine times in these four verses.
God sent “his only Son” (v. 9). The word means the one and only of his kind. John uses it of the Son in his Gospel too (1:14, 18; 3:16, 18). The gift is measured by what it cost.

The means by which sin is taken away and communion with God restored (v. 10; also 2:2). It recalls the Day of Atonement. John does not picture an angry God being won over: it is God who loves first and who himself sends the Son.
vv: Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God;
John does not first say “love, because it is commanded”, but “love, because love comes from God”. To love is to let God’s own life pass through us.
Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love.

Knowing God here is not having information about him but sharing his life. John does not say that love is God; he says that God is love. The one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is in his very being love.
God sent his only Son into the world so that we might live through him.
Love is revealed not in a feeling but in a sending, and the purpose is life.
In this is love, not that we loved God but that he loved us
Every Christian life begins by being loved. We do not earn God’s love by our love; our love is the answer to his.
ch: Pope Benedict XVI began his first encyclical, Deus Caritas Est (2005), with 1 John 4:16, which repeats today’s v. 8, and said that these words express with remarkable clarity the heart of the Christian faith (in substance). The Catechism teaches that in saying “God is love” John affirms that God’s very being is love, and that by sending his Son and the Spirit, God has revealed his innermost secret: he himself is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit (CCC 221). It quotes v. 10 to show that the Father’s giving up of his Son for our sins comes from love that goes before any merit of ours (CCC 604).

r.h: I have called you friends
set: The Last Supper, just after the image of the vine and the branches (15:1–8). Jesus now says plainly what the sap of the vine is: his love, which he has received from the Father. The passage moves from love received (v. 9), to love kept (v. 10), to love given away (vv. 12–13), and ends where it began, with the command to love (v. 17).
He speaks on the night before he dies. When he says that no one has greater love than to lay down one’s life for one’s friends (v. 13), he is describing what he will do the next day.
str: v. 9: as the Father has loved me; abide in my love.
vv. 10–11: keeping the commandments, and joy made complete.
vv. 12–13: love one another as I have loved you; the greatest love.
vv. 14–15: no longer servants but friends.
vv. 16–17: chosen and appointed to bear fruit that will last; love one another.
kw: Not an equal in power, but one with whom a person shares his heart (v. 15). In the Old Testament Abraham is called God’s friend (Isaiah 41:8; see James 2:23), and the Lord spoke with Moses as one speaks to a friend (Exodus 33:11). What was given to a few is now given to all the disciples.
To remain, to make one’s home (vv. 9–10). Love here is not a passing moment but a dwelling place.
Joy is the purpose of his words (v. 11). It is his own joy, which does not depend on circumstances, and which, in the same discourse, he says no one will take from them (16:22).
vv: As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.
The love the disciples receive is the same love that flows between the Father and the Son. Nothing less is offered.
This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.
The “as” is both the measure and the source. We cannot love as he did by our own strength; we can love because he has first loved us.
No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
St Paul goes further still: Christ died for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8). The friends for whom Jesus dies include those who will deny and abandon him that very night.
I do not call you servants any longer,

Being a servant of God is no disgrace; Paul proudly calls himself a servant of Christ Jesus (Romans 1:1). But a servant is told what to do, while a friend is told why. Jesus has shared with them all that he has heard from the Father.
You did not choose me but I chose you.
Usually a disciple chose his teacher. Here the Teacher chooses. A vocation begins with being chosen, and so it rests more on his faithfulness than on ours.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 9 and 12 when it teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment: by loving one another the disciples imitate the love of Jesus which they themselves receive (CCC 1823). St Thomas Aquinas, appealing to v. 15, teaches that charity is a friendship of man with God (Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 23, a. 1, in substance). The Church sees the fullest form of v. 13 in the martyrs, and also in every hidden life spent for others.

qa: Does “God shows no partiality” mean that all religions are the same?

No. Peter says it and then preaches Christ and baptises. The Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions and sees in them, often, a ray of the Truth that enlightens all people; at the same time she proclaims Christ, the way, the truth and the life, in whom people find the fullness of religious life (Nostra Aetate 2). God’s welcome to every nation is the reason for the mission, not a reason to give it up.
If “God is love”, how can there be judgment?

Love is not indifference. A love that did not care whether we lived or destroyed ourselves would not be love. The same passage says that God sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins (4:10): God takes sin seriously because he loves. The Church teaches that only one who finally and of his own will refuses that merciful love remains separated from him (CCC 1033).
Jesus says “I chose you”. Did he not choose everyone?

At the Supper he speaks first to the Twelve, whom he chose and appointed to go and bear fruit. But every Christian is chosen in Christ (Ephesians 1:4), and the call is offered to all. To be chosen is not a privilege to keep for oneself, but a sending: “to go and bear fruit”.
rite: In India the Solemnity of the Ascension is kept next Sunday, 9 May. The days between the Ascension and Pentecost recall the apostles devoted to prayer together with Mary the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14), the prayer from which the Pentecost novena takes its pattern. Peter’s question about the water of baptism makes this a good Sunday for the rite of blessing and sprinkling of water, which the Roman Missal allows in place of the penitential act on Sundays, especially in Easter Time. On Thursday and Friday of last week the weekday Mass read the two halves of today’s Gospel (John 15:9–11 and 15:12–17); today they are heard together, with John’s letter as their commentary.
study: Where have I seen God at work in someone before they knew him, as he was in Cornelius?
John says that love begins with God’s love for us. When did I last simply let myself be loved by God, in prayer or in confession?
Jesus calls me his friend, not his servant. How would my prayer change if I spoke to him as a friend?
For whom am I being asked to lay down a little of my life this week: my time, my pride, my comfort?

lead: Today the Church keeps the Feast of Saints Philip and James, Apostles. The first reading gives the oldest summary of the Gospel in the New Testament: Christ died, was buried, was raised, and appeared; and one of those to whom he appeared was James. The Gospel shows Philip at the Last Supper, asking what every human heart asks: “Lord, show us the Father.” Psalm 19 says that the voice of the heavens goes out through all the earth; the voice of the apostles went with it.

Why the two together? According to tradition, their relics were placed in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Rome, dedicated in the sixth century, and the shared feast grew from that dedication. Philip of Bethsaida and James son of Alphaeus are among the less known of the Twelve, yet the Church is built on them too.

r.h: Then he appeared to James
set: Paul writes to Corinth in the mid-50s. Some there were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead (15:12). Before answering them, Paul reminds them of the Gospel they received, on which they stand. These verses contain an early formula of faith which Paul himself had received. Many scholars think it goes back to the first years after the Resurrection.

Background. The James of v. 7 is James the brother of the Lord, leader of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19; Acts 15:13). In the Bible “brother” can mean a close relative, and the Church understands it so here (CCC 500). The Latin tradition, following St Jerome, identified this James with the apostle James son of Alphaeus, and that is why this reading is chosen for today. Many scholars distinguish the two, and the Eastern tradition generally keeps them apart; the Church has not settled the question by definition.
str: vv. 1–2: the Gospel you received, in which you stand and through which you are being saved.
vv. 3–5: the formula: died, buried, raised, appeared to Cephas and to the Twelve.
vv. 6–7: more than five hundred at once; James; all the apostles.
v. 8: last of all, to Paul.
kw: The technical words for passing on a tradition (v. 3; the same pair introduces the Lord’s Supper in 11:23). Paul does not invent the Gospel; he received it and hands it on. This is what the Church calls apostolic Tradition.
Said twice (vv. 3, 4). The death and Resurrection of Christ are not accidents of history but the fulfilment of God’s plan foretold in the Scriptures of Israel.
Four times in these verses (vv. 5, 6, 7, 8). The Risen One lets himself be seen. The witnesses do not produce the experience; they receive it.
A child born out of time (v. 8). Paul uses a hard word of himself: he came to faith late, and as a persecutor.
vv: For I handed on to you as of first importance what I in turn had received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures,

The same words of handing on and receiving introduce the account of the Lord’s Supper (11:23). Faith in the Resurrection and the Eucharist reach us by the same road: the living Tradition of the Church.
and that he was buried,
A short phrase with weight. The burial confirms that the death was real, and it stands behind the Gospel accounts of the empty tomb.
Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time, most of whom are still alive,
Almost an invitation to check: the witnesses could still be asked. Paul is not repeating a legend from long ago.
Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

The Gospels do not narrate this appearance. During the ministry the brothers of the Lord did not believe in him (John 7:5); after the Resurrection they are found praying with the apostles and with Mary (Acts 1:14). An appearance of the Risen Lord to James may lie behind that change.
Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.
Paul counts his meeting with Christ on the road to Damascus among the appearances, though it came later than the others.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 3–4 to show how early the faith in the Resurrection was handed on (CCC 639). It also notes that Peter and the Twelve are the first witnesses of the Resurrection, but not the only ones: Paul speaks of more than five hundred, of James, and of all the apostles (CCC 642). The Second Vatican Council teaches that what the apostles handed on grows in understanding in the Church, with the help of the Holy Spirit, without ceasing to be the same faith (Dei Verbum 8).

r.h: Lord, show us the Father
set: At the Last Supper Jesus has said that he is going to prepare a place for his disciples and that they know the way (14:1–4). Thomas objects that they do not even know where he is going (14:5). Jesus answers with one of his great “I am” sayings, and then Philip speaks.

Background. Philip came from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter (1:44). Jesus called him with the words “Follow me”, and Philip at once went to bring Nathanael (1:43–46). Before the feeding of the five thousand Jesus tested him by asking where they could buy bread (6:5–7), and it was to Philip that some Greeks came, wishing to see Jesus (12:20–22). In John, Philip is the disciple of plain questions and of bringing others to Jesus.
str: v. 6: I am the way, and the truth, and the life.
v. 7: to know me is to know the Father.
vv. 8–11: Philip’s request, and the answer: whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
vv. 12–14: greater works, and prayer in his name.
kw: A road, and also a way of life. The first Christians were called those who belonged to “the Way” (Acts 9:2). Jesus does not only show the way; he is the way.
In John, truth is the faithful reality of God made known. Jesus does not only speak true things; he is the truth in person (v. 6).
To ask in his name (vv. 13–14) is not to add a formula, but to ask as one united with him, for what he wills. That is why the prayers of the Mass end “through our Lord Jesus Christ”.
vv: I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
Three words, one person. St Augustine taught that Christ is our homeland as God and our way as man: we go through him to him (in substance).
Lord, show us the Father, and we will be satisfied.

Philip’s request is the longing of the whole Bible. Moses once asked to see the glory of God (Exodus 33:18). Philip asks well; what he has not yet grasped is that the answer is standing in front of him.
Have I been with you all this time, Philip, and you still do not know me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.
Less a rebuke than a sigh of love. Philip had been with him for years, and there was still more to know. So it is with us.
the one who believes in me will also do the works that I do and, in fact, will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.

Not greater in power than the raising of Lazarus, but greater in reach: after Pentecost the Gospel goes through the apostles to the nations. The reason is “because I am going to the Father”: the works of the Church are his works, done through the Spirit he sends.
ch: The Second Vatican Council quotes v. 9 to teach that Jesus completes and perfects revelation: to see him is to see the Father (Dei Verbum 4). The Catechism says the same of his whole earthly life, his words and deeds, his silences and sufferings: all of it reveals the Father (CCC 516). Ancient tradition honours St James, identified in the West with the Lord’s brother, as the first bishop of Jerusalem, and remembers St Philip as having preached in Asia Minor and died at Hierapolis in Phrygia.

qa: Does “No one comes to the Father except through me” mean that only baptised Christians can be saved?

Christ is the one way to the Father; there is no other name by which we are saved (Acts 4:12). But the Church also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ and his Church, yet seek God with a sincere heart and, moved by grace, try to do his will, can attain salvation (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). Whoever is saved is saved through Christ, even without yet knowing his name. That is why the Church still has the duty to proclaim him to all (CCC 848).
Which James is this? There are several in the New Testament.

There is James son of Zebedee, brother of John (feast 25 July); James son of Alphaeus, one of the Twelve; and James the brother of the Lord, leader of the church in Jerusalem, a close relative of Jesus and not a son of Mary (CCC 500). The Latin tradition, following St Jerome, identified the second and the third, and honours him today with Philip. He is often called James the Less, from Mark’s “James the younger” (Mark 15:40). Many scholars, and the Eastern Churches, distinguish them. The Letter of James is traditionally linked with the brother of the Lord.
rite: Both apostles are named among the saints in the first Eucharistic Prayer, the Roman Canon. Their feast has its own Gloria and the Preface of the Apostles; the Creed is not said, since it is a feast and not a solemnity. Since 1969 the feast has been kept on 3 May. Earlier it was kept on 1 May, and from 1955 on 11 May, when 1 May was given to St Joseph the Worker.
study: Paul received the faith and handed it on. Who handed it on to me, and to whom am I handing it on?
Philip asked a plain question and received a deep answer. What plain question would I ask Jesus today?
Where do I see the Father in the face and deeds of Jesus in the Gospels?
James was once among the relatives who did not believe. What does his story say to families where some do not yet believe?

lead: At Philippi Paul and Silas are stripped, beaten and fastened in the stocks, and at midnight they are singing hymns. An earthquake opens the doors, but the real liberation is the jailer’s: before morning he and his household are baptised and rejoicing at table. In the Gospel Jesus tells his grieving disciples that his going away is for their good, because the Advocate will come. Psalm 138 gives thanks to the Lord whose right hand delivers.

r.h: What must I do to be saved?
set: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, proud of its Roman law and its settled veterans. There Paul had baptised Lydia and her household (16:14–15). Then he freed a slave girl from a spirit of divination, and her owners, who had made money from her, dragged Paul and Silas before the magistrates (16:16–21). Today’s reading begins with the punishment. Later in the chapter Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens, who should never have been beaten without a trial (16:37).
str: vv. 22–24: beaten and thrown into the innermost cell.
vv. 25–26: hymns at midnight, and the earthquake.
vv. 27–30: the jailer’s despair and his question.
vv. 31–34: the word, the washing of wounds, baptism and the meal.
kw: The jailer’s question (v. 30) may at first have meant “How do I get out of this?” Paul answers it at its deepest level: salvation through faith in the Lord Jesus.
“You and your household” (v. 31). In the ancient world a household took in the family, the children and the servants. In Acts whole households come to faith together (16:15; 18:8).
Paul and Silas pray and sing (v. 25) with their backs torn and their feet in the stocks. Praise in the dark becomes a witness: the other prisoners were listening.
vv: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
Their praise does not depend on their circumstances. Many prisoners for Christ since then, in many lands, have done the same.
But Paul shouted in a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.”
A guard who lost his prisoners could expect to pay with his own life. The apostles could have walked away. They stay, and by staying they save a life before they save a soul.
“Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
Faith is the door. It does not stand against baptism: in the next verses the whole household hears the word of the Lord and is baptised (vv. 32–33).
At the same hour of the night he took them and washed their wounds; then he and his entire family were baptized without delay.
Two washings in one hour: he washes their wounds, and he himself is washed in baptism. New faith shows itself at once in mercy.
ch: The Catechism points to the household baptisms of Acts when it explains that infant baptism is an immemorial tradition of the Church: there is explicit testimony from the second century on, and it is quite possible that when whole households received baptism, infants were baptised too (CCC 1252). The jailer’s question, “What must I do to be saved?”, is the question the Church answers in every preparation for baptism: hear the word, believe, be baptised, and live in joy.

r.h: It is to your advantage that I go away
set: The farewell discourse continues. Jesus has warned the disciples that hard times are coming for them (16:1–4). Now he speaks of his going, and they are filled with sorrow. Earlier Peter and Thomas had asked where he was going (13:36; 14:5). Now no one asks; grief has silenced them.
str: vv. 5–6: I am going, and sorrow fills your hearts.
v. 7: it is for your good; the Advocate will come.
vv. 8–11: the Spirit will prove the world wrong about sin, righteousness and judgment.
kw: One called to stand beside another: a counsel for the defence, a helper, a comforter (v. 7). In the Gospels only John uses this title, always of the Spirit (14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7); his first letter uses it of Jesus himself (1 John 2:1).

A word of the law court: to expose, to bring to light, to convince (v. 8). In the trial between Jesus and the world, the world thought it had judged him. The Spirit shows that the verdict was the other way round.
The same word Caiaphas used when he said that it was better for one man to die for the people (11:50). He spoke more truly than he knew. Jesus’ going brings good to all.
vv: But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your hearts.
Jesus does not scold their sorrow. He names it, and then gives them a reason for hope.
it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you;
In his earthly body he was in one place at a time. Through the Spirit he will be present everywhere, and within every disciple.
about sin, because they do not believe in me;
For John the root sin is refusing the light that has come into the world (3:19). The Spirit brings it to light, not to crush, but so that the world may turn and believe.
ch: St John Paul II made this passage the centre of his encyclical on the Holy Spirit, Dominum et Vivificantem (1986), dwelling on the Spirit who convinces the world concerning sin. He teaches that the Spirit convinces of sin in order to save: the conviction opens the way to conversion and to the forgiveness that flows from the Cross (in substance). The Catechism, too, speaks of the Spirit who reveals sin and at the same time gives the grace of repentance (CCC 1433).

qa: How can it be better for the disciples that Jesus goes away?

He does not leave them alone. He goes to the Father and sends the Spirit, who makes him present in a new and deeper way: not beside them, but within them, and in the word and sacraments of the Church. The Ascension is not an absence but a new kind of presence.
study: Paul and Silas sang at midnight. What helps me to pray when things are dark?
What sorrow in me might Jesus be turning toward the gift of his Spirit?

lead: Paul stands in Athens, the city of philosophers, and begins not with condemnation but with an altar “to an unknown god”. He proclaims the God they half knew, and then the Resurrection, and many walk away. In the Gospel Jesus says that he has more to tell than the disciples can bear now; the Spirit of truth will guide them into all the truth. Psalm 148 calls kings and peoples, young and old, to praise the name of the Lord.

r.h: To an unknown god
set: Driven out of Thessalonica and then Beroea, Paul is brought to Athens and waits there for Silas and Timothy. Athens was no longer a great power, but it was still a famous city of learning. Paul is deeply distressed at the many idols (17:16). He argues in the synagogue and in the marketplace, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers take him for a preacher of foreign gods (17:17–18). Some scholars think they even took “Jesus and the resurrection”, Anastasis, for a pair of new gods. They bring him to the Areopagus.

Background. The Areopagus, the hill of Ares, gave its name to an ancient council of the city, still respected in Roman times. Paul’s speech there is not a defence at a trial, but a public account of his teaching before the city’s leading men.
str: v. 15: Paul is brought to Athens.
vv. 22–23: the altar to an unknown god.
vv. 24–28: the God who made all things, gives life to all, and is near to each one.
vv. 29–31: not like gold or stone; the call to repent; the day of judgment and the man raised from the dead.
17:32–18:1: mockery, delay, and a few believers; Paul goes on to Corinth.
kw: Paul calls the Athenians “extremely religious” (v. 22). The word can mean devout or superstitious; Paul begins with the respectful sense. He builds a bridge before he crosses it.
Ancient writers mention altars at Athens to unknown gods. Paul takes the inscription as an honest confession of ignorance and offers to fill it (v. 23).

The word that divided his hearers (v. 32). Many Greeks could accept that the soul survives death, but the rising of the dead seemed foolish to them. Paul later writes that Christ crucified is foolishness to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23).
vv: What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.
Paul does not mock their search. He honours it, and then gives it a name.
For ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are his offspring.’

Paul quotes Greek poets, not the Hebrew Scriptures, which his hearers do not know. The second line comes from the poet Aratus; the first is often traced to Epimenides of Crete, though that is less certain. Truth found in pagan poetry can become a step toward Christ.
now he commands all people everywhere to repent,
The bridge has a far side. Respect for their search does not mean leaving them where they are. The God they sought now calls them to turn to him.
When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some scoffed; but others said, “We will hear you again about this.”
Three responses: mockery, delay, and faith (v. 34). They are still the responses to preaching today.
But some of them joined him and became believers, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris,

Few, but real. Tradition makes Dionysius the first bishop of Athens. Writings that later circulated under his name are now generally dated to around the year 500; they had great influence on Christian mystical theology.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 28 when it teaches that God, the Creator, is present to the inmost being of his creatures (CCC 300). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, which often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all people, while she proclaims Christ, the way, the truth and the life (Nostra Aetate 2). St Justin Martyr, a philosopher who became a Christian, spoke of the seeds of the Word sown among all peoples (in substance), and the Council uses the same image (Ad Gentes 11). Paul at the Areopagus shows the way: respect, common ground, and then the clear proclamation of the Risen Christ.

r.h: He will guide you into all the truth
set: Still at the Last Supper. Jesus knows that the disciples cannot yet carry the full weight of what is coming: the Cross, the Resurrection, the mission to the nations. He does not overload them. He promises the Spirit, who will lead them step by step.
str: v. 12: many things you cannot bear now.
v. 13: the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth.
vv. 14–15: he will glorify me, taking what is mine; all that the Father has is mine.
kw: To lead along a road (v. 13). The Spirit does not hand over the truth all at once like a parcel; he walks with the Church into it.
They cannot “bear” it now (v. 12). The word is used of carrying a load, as Jesus carried his cross (19:17).
Three times in vv. 13–15. The Spirit announces and makes known. What he declares is not a new revelation beside Christ, but what belongs to Christ.
vv: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
The patience of a good teacher. God gives light as we are able to receive it.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth;
Not into new truths that contradict Christ, but ever more deeply into the one truth that is Christ.
All that the Father has is mine.
One of the clearest glimpses of the Trinity in the Gospels: the Father gives all to the Son, and the Spirit takes from the Son and declares it to us.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Tradition which comes from the apostles develops in the Church with the help of the Holy Spirit: there is a growth in the understanding of the realities and the words handed on, and the Spirit leads believers into all truth (Dei Verbum 8). St John Henry Newman, in his work on the development of doctrine, showed how the Church grows in understanding without changing the faith. Development is not a change of the faith but its deeper understanding.

qa: Did Paul fail at Athens?

Some have thought so, because few believed, and because Paul later says that he came to Corinth in weakness, resolved to know nothing but Jesus Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:1–3). But Luke does not present the speech as a failure: there were believers, and a man and a woman are named among them. Faithfulness, not numbers, is the measure.
study: What “unknown god” do the people around me seek, and how could I begin from their search, as Paul did?
Is there something in the faith I could not bear before, but understand better now?

lead: Paul arrives in Corinth, a busy port city, and finds a Jewish couple, Aquila and Priscilla, who share his trade. He works with his hands during the week and argues in the synagogue every sabbath. In the Gospel Jesus speaks of “a little while”: the disciples will weep, and then their pain will turn into joy. Psalm 98 sings again that the Lord has made known his victory before the nations.

r.h: They worked together
set: Corinth, refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar, was the capital of the province of Achaia, a crowded trading city between two seas. Paul stayed there a year and six months (18:11). An inscription found at Delphi names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia (see 18:12), and it allows Paul’s stay to be dated to about AD 50–52, one of the firmest dates in his life.

Background. The Roman historian Suetonius writes that Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews who were constantly causing disturbances at the instigation of “Chrestus”. Many scholars think this refers to disputes about Christ within the Jewish community of Rome, and date the expulsion to about AD 49. Aquila and Priscilla may already have been Christians when Paul met them.
str: vv. 1–3: Paul comes to Corinth and works with Aquila and Priscilla.
v. 4: every sabbath in the synagogue.
v. 5: Silas and Timothy arrive; Paul gives himself wholly to the word.
v. 6: opposition, and Paul turns to the Gentiles.
vv. 7–8: the house of Titius Justus; Crispus and many Corinthians believe.
kw: Only here in the New Testament (v. 3). It may mean a worker in leather or in cloth; tents were made of both. Paul was proud to support himself by his own work (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 9:15–18).
Reasoned discussion, not shouting (v. 4). The same word describes Paul’s practice at Thessalonica (17:2) and at Athens (17:17).
The leader responsible for the synagogue’s worship (v. 8). Crispus is one of the very few people Paul says he baptised himself (1 Corinthians 1:14).
vv: There he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla,

Paul later greets them as those who work with him in Christ Jesus and who risked their necks for his life; a church met in their house (Romans 16:3–5). A married couple stands at the heart of the early mission.
he stayed with them, and they worked together
The apostle shares a workshop. The Gospel was spoken over the cutting of leather and the stitching of cloth, as well as in the synagogue.
Every sabbath he would argue in the synagogue and would try to convince Jews and Greeks.
Paul goes first to the synagogue, as always: to Israel belong the covenants and the promises (Romans 9:4). The “Greeks” here are probably Gentiles who worshipped with the synagogue.
“Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”

Strong words, but they echo the watchman of Ezekiel 33: having given warning, the watchman is not responsible (Ezekiel 33:4–9). They are not a curse on a people. In the next verses the synagogue official Crispus believes, and in the next city Paul again goes first to the synagogue (18:19).
ch: The Second Vatican Council, speaking of the apostolate of lay people, recalls the men and women who helped Paul in spreading the Gospel, among them Aquila and Priscilla (Apostolicam Actuositatem 10, in substance). St John Paul II, in Laborem Exercens (1981), taught that through work a person shares in the activity of the Creator. Paul the tentmaker shows that daily labour and the preaching of the Gospel are not rivals.

r.h: Your pain will turn into joy
set: The Last Supper. Jesus speaks a riddle: “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.” The disciples repeat it among themselves, puzzled. Jesus, knowing what they want to ask, answers not with an explanation but with a promise.
str: v. 16: the riddle of “a little while”.
vv. 17–18: the disciples’ confusion.
vv. 19–20: weeping now, joy to come.
kw: Seven times in these five verses. The first “little while” leads to the Cross and the tomb; the second to Easter. The Fathers also heard in it the whole time of the Church, short when measured against eternity.
Grief of heart (v. 20). In the next verse Jesus compares it to the pain of a woman in labour, which gives way to the joy of a child born.
Not sorrow replaced by joy from outside, but sorrow itself “turned into” joy (v. 20). The same Cross that caused their tears becomes the source of their joy.
vv: “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me.”
Within hours they will not see him, for he is arrested, crucified and buried. On the third day they will see him risen.
We do not know what he is talking about.
An honest confession, and the Gospel does not hide it. Not understanding is not the same as not believing.
you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice; you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
The disciples’ tears are not wasted. God does not only take sorrow away; he transforms it.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on this Gospel, says that this “little while” is the whole span of the present age: it seems long to us while it lasts, but when it is over we shall see how short it was (in substance). The Church lives in that second little while, between the Ascension and the Lord’s return, with real tears and a joy that no one can take away (16:22).

qa: Did Paul turn his back on his own people at Corinth?

No. He moved next door, to the house of Titius Justus beside the synagogue (v. 7), and the synagogue official himself became a believer (v. 8). Paul’s words are a prophet’s protest that he has done his duty, not a rejection of the Jewish people. He later writes that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2), and the Church teaches the same (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: In many countries Thursday 6 May is the Solemnity of the Ascension. In India it is transferred to Sunday 9 May, so today the Easter weekday readings are read. The words “a little while, and you will no longer see me” prepare us well for the Ascension that is near.
study: Paul worked with his hands and preached the word. How can my daily work become part of my witness?
What sorrow in my life am I asking God to turn into joy, and not only to take away?

lead: Paul at Corinth is told in a vision not to be afraid, and he stays a year and a half. When a case is brought against him, the Roman governor refuses to hear it, and the word goes on. In the Gospel Jesus tells the disciples that their sorrow will be like the pain of a woman in labour: real, but turned into a joy that no one can take away. Psalm 47 sings of God, king of all the earth, the Lord whose kingdom the apostle is carrying into the cities of Greece.

r.h: Do not be afraid, but speak
set: Paul came to Corinth after Athens (18:1). He found work and lodging with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome by the emperor Claudius, who were tentmakers like himself (18:2–3). When many in the synagogue would not accept his message, he moved next door to the house of Titius Justus. Crispus, the official of the synagogue, believed with all his household (18:4–8). Corinth was a large, rich port city, the capital of the Roman province of Achaia.

Background. An inscription found at Delphi, a letter of the emperor Claudius, names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia. From it scholars date his term to about AD 51–52, and this gives one of the surest dates in the life of Paul. Gallio was the brother of the philosopher Seneca.
str: vv. 9–11: the vision at night, and Paul stays a year and six months.
vv. 12–13: some opponents bring Paul before Gallio’s tribunal.
vv. 14–16: Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about their own law.
v. 17: Sosthenes is beaten, and Gallio takes no notice.
v. 18: Paul sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila; the vow at Cenchreae.
kw: The word spoken to Abraham, to Mary, to the shepherds, and now to Paul. It is not a promise that nothing will hurt; it is a promise of presence: “for I am with you”.

The governor of a senatorial province such as Achaia. Luke uses the exact title, as he does for Sergius Paulus in Cyprus (13:7). Such accurate titles are one reason historians take Luke’s account seriously.

The raised platform from which a Roman magistrate gave judgment. A large stone platform of this kind still stands in the forum of ancient Corinth. Paul later wrote to the Corinthians that all of us must appear before the judgment seat (bēma) of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).
vv: “Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent;
Paul had arrived in Corinth, as he says himself, “in weakness and in fear and in much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). The Lord meets the fear of the preacher at night, before it can silence him.
for there are many in this city who are my people.
The Lord already counts as his own people many in Corinth who have not yet heard the Gospel. The missionary does not bring God to a city; he finds God already at work there.
see to it yourselves; I do not wish to be a judge of these matters.

Luke means a particular group of opponents in Corinth, not the Jewish people, and the synagogue official Crispus had already believed (18:8). Gallio sees only a quarrel about words and names. His indifference becomes a protection: for the time being, Roman law will not forbid the preaching.
At Cenchreae he had his hair cut, for he was under a vow.

Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth (Phoebe was a minister (diakonos) of its church, Romans 16:1). The vow was probably a private vow of thanksgiving of the Nazirite kind (Numbers 6). Paul the apostle of the Gentiles still keeps the devout practices of his own people.
ch: The Church has always read the vision at Corinth as a word to every preacher and catechist: fear is not a reason to be silent, because the Lord is with those he sends. The same promise closes Matthew’s Gospel: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20). Paul’s long stay at Corinth gave rise to two of his greatest letters, 1 and 2 Corinthians. The names in this chapter, Priscilla, Aquila, Crispus and perhaps Sosthenes, who is named with Paul at the start of 1 Corinthians, remind us that the Gospel was carried by households and friendships, not by one man alone.

r.h: Your pain will turn into joy
set: We are at the Last Supper, near the end of the farewell discourse. Jesus has just said, “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me” (16:16), and the disciples do not understand. He answers with a picture every family knows: a woman in labour.
str: v. 20: you will weep, the world will rejoice; your pain will turn into joy.
v. 21: the woman in labour and the joy of the child born.
v. 22: “I will see you again”, and a joy no one will take away.
v. 23: on that day you will ask nothing of me; the Father will give in my name.
kw: The same word for the disciples’ grief and the mother’s pain. The sorrow is not denied or hurried over. It is turned, the very same sorrow, into joy.
In John “the hour” is the hour of Jesus’ Passion and glory (2:4; 12:23; 13:1). Here the mother has her hour too: the Cross is pictured as a birth.
Jesus’ joy runs through the discourse: “so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete” (15:11). It does not depend on what the world gives or takes.
vv: you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
Jesus does not say that joy will replace the pain, as if it were simply forgotten. The pain itself will be changed, as Good Friday becomes the way to Easter.
When a woman is in labor, she has pain, because her hour has come.

The prophets used the same picture for the coming of God’s new age: Zion in labour giving birth to a new people (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14). Many Christian readers have also seen here the Church, and Mary at the foot of the Cross, becoming mother in sorrow.
and no one will take your joy from you.
Easter joy is not a mood. It rests on a fact: “I will see you again”. What rests on the Risen Lord cannot be taken by any persecutor or loss.
ch: The Church reads this Gospel in the Easter season because it explains the Easter experience from the inside: the disciples’ grief on Good Friday and their joy on Easter morning (20:20). The Second Vatican Council opens its constitution on the Church in the modern world with the words “the joys and the hopes, the griefs and the anxieties” of the people of this age, which are also those of the followers of Christ (Gaudium et Spes 1). Christian joy does not ignore sorrow; it carries it to the Lord, who turns it.

qa: Does Christian joy mean we should not grieve?

No. Jesus says plainly, “you will weep and mourn”. He wept himself at the tomb of Lazarus (11:35). The promise is not that we will never grieve, but that our grief is not the end. It will be turned into a joy that no one can take.
study: What fear keeps me silent when I should speak of my faith? What does the Lord’s “I am with you” change?
Which sorrow in my life am I being asked to give to the Lord, so that he may turn it into joy?

lead: Apollos, a gifted preacher from Alexandria, teaches accurately about Jesus but knows only John’s baptism, and a married couple, Priscilla and Aquila, take him aside and explain the Way more accurately. In the Gospel Jesus teaches the disciples to ask the Father in his name and tells them that the Father himself loves them. He ends: “I am leaving the world and am going to the Father.” Psalm 47 sings of God who has gone up with a shout, and it prepares the Ascension, which the Church in India keeps this Sunday.

r.h: They explained the Way of God more accurately
set: Today’s reading begins the third great journey of Paul. After a short visit to Antioch in Syria, he sets out again through Galatia and Phrygia, the region of his earlier churches, strengthening the disciples (v. 23). Luke then turns to Ephesus, where Priscilla and Aquila had stayed when Paul passed through (18:19), and introduces a new figure.

Background. Alexandria in Egypt had a large and learned Jewish community. The Jewish Scriptures had been translated into Greek there (the Septuagint), and the Jewish philosopher Philo taught there in the time of Jesus. An Alexandrian Jew “well-versed in the scriptures” would have known how to read them carefully and eloquently.
str: v. 23: Paul strengthens the disciples of Galatia and Phrygia.
vv. 24–25: Apollos at Ephesus: eloquent, fervent, but knowing only John’s baptism.
v. 26: Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and teach him.
vv. 27–28: Apollos goes to Achaia and helps the believers there.
kw: An early name for the Christian faith and community in Acts (9:2; 19:9, 23; 24:14). Faith is not only a set of ideas but a road to walk, the way of the Lord.

The NRSV has “with burning enthusiasm”. The words can mean his own fervent spirit, or the Holy Spirit; Paul uses the same phrase in Romans 12:11. Zeal and learning are both gifts, and both need to be guided.

Apollos taught “accurately” (v. 25), yet Priscilla and Aquila explained the Way to him “more accurately” (v. 26). It is the same word Luke uses in the prologue of his Gospel (Luke 1:3). Good teaching can always grow more complete.
vv: He was an eloquent man, well-versed in the scriptures.

Apollos became well known in Corinth. Some there even boasted “I belong to Apollos” (1 Corinthians 1:12). Paul does not blame Apollos for this: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6).
though he knew only the baptism of John.

He knew the preaching of repentance and the facts about Jesus, but perhaps not yet the full gift of the Spirit and the baptism in the name of Jesus. Monday’s reading will show a group at Ephesus in the same position.
they took him aside and explained the Way of God to him more accurately.

They did not correct him in public. They took him aside, probably into their home. Priscilla is named first here, as in several other places; she was clearly a teacher of the faith alongside her husband.
showing by the scriptures that the Messiah is Jesus.
This was a debate among Jews about how to read their own Scriptures. The early Church’s preaching always began here: the Law and the Prophets point to Christ (Luke 24:27).
ch: The Church sees in Priscilla and Aquila a model of the lay apostolate and of the Christian family as a place of formation. Paul calls them his co-workers who risked their necks for him, and greets “the church in their house” (Romans 16:3–5). The Second Vatican Council, in its decree on the apostolate of the laity, names Aquila and Priscilla among the men and women who helped Paul in spreading the Gospel (Apostolicam Actuositatem 10). Apollos, for his part, shows the humility of a great preacher who is willing to be taught.

r.h: The Father himself loves you
set: The farewell discourse at the Last Supper draws to a close. Jesus has spoken of his going away and of the disciples’ sorrow turned into joy. Now he speaks of what will change on “that day”, the day of his resurrection and of the gift of the Spirit: they will pray to the Father in his name, and they will know the Father’s love directly.
str: vv. 23b–24: ask the Father in my name, and your joy will be complete.
v. 25: from figures of speech to plain speech about the Father.
vv. 26–27: the Father himself loves you.
v. 28: from the Father into the world, and from the world to the Father.
kw: To ask in his name is not a formula added at the end of a prayer. It is to pray as one united with him, in his person, for what he wills.
A veiled saying or parable, like the shepherd (10:6) and the woman in labour. After the resurrection the disciples will understand plainly, through the Spirit who teaches them.
In v. 27 John uses the word for the love of friends: the Father loves them as friends because they have loved the Son. Jesus has already called them friends (15:15).
vv: Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.
The purpose of prayer is not only to obtain things but to have complete joy, which is communion with the Father.
I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;

This does not deny that Christ intercedes for us; Hebrews 7:25 says that he always lives to make intercession. It means that the disciples are not kept at a distance. United with the Son, they come to the Father themselves.
for the Father himself loves you,
The Father does not have to be persuaded to love us by the Son. The Son came because the Father already loved the world (3:16).
I came from the Father and have come into the world; again, I am leaving the world and am going to the Father.
The whole mystery of Christ in one sentence: from the Father, into the world, and back to the Father. It is the road of the Ascension, which the Church celebrates on Sunday.
ch: The Catechism teaches that prayer in the name of Jesus is new with the resurrection, and quotes v. 24 on asking in his name (CCC 2614–2615). This is why the prayers of the Mass end “through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son”. St Augustine teaches that we ask in the name of the Saviour when we ask for what belongs to our salvation (in substance). Verse 28 is a short creed of the Incarnation and the Ascension: the Son who came down returns to the Father, and he takes our human nature with him.

qa: Why does God not always give what I ask in Jesus’ name?

To ask in his name is to ask as he would ask, for what truly serves salvation. The Catechism says that God, who knows what we need, sometimes delays or gives something better, and that we must persevere in trusting prayer (CCC 2735–2737). The promise is sure: the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).
study: Who has taken me aside, as Priscilla and Aquila did for Apollos, to help me know the faith more accurately? Whom could I help in the same way?
When I pray, do I come to God as a stranger who needs to persuade him, or as one whom the Father himself loves?

lead: In India, as in many countries, the Solemnity of the Ascension of the Lord is kept on this Sunday, in place of the Seventh Sunday of Easter. Three readings tell one mystery from three sides. Acts tells the event: forty days, the promise of the Spirit, the cloud and the two men in white. Ephesians tells its meaning: God raised Christ and seated him at his right hand, far above every power, as head of the Church, his body. Mark tells its fruit: the apostles go out and preach everywhere, and the Lord works with them.

Psalm 47 gives the cry of the day: “God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Psalm 47:5). The psalm may first have accompanied the Ark of the Covenant going up to the Temple. The Church hears in it the Risen Lord going up to the Father. For the second reading the Lectionary also allows Ephesians 4:1–13, on the gifts of the ascended Christ to his Church.

r.h: As they were watching, he was lifted up
set: The Acts of the Apostles is the second volume of Luke’s work. It is addressed, like the Gospel, to Theophilus (Luke 1:3). The “first book” is the Gospel, which also ends with the Ascension, at Bethany, with the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy (Luke 24:50–53). Luke tells the Ascension twice: at the end of the Gospel, as the close of Jesus’ earthly life, and at the start of Acts, as the beginning of the Church’s mission.

Background. In the Old Testament the cloud is the sign of God’s presence and glory: the pillar of cloud in the desert (Exodus 13:21), the cloud on Sinai (Exodus 24:15–18), the cloud filling the Temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). In Daniel 7:13 one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient One. Elijah was taken up to heaven, and Elisha received a double share of his spirit because he saw him go (2 Kings 2:9–15). The number forty recalls Israel’s forty years in the desert and Jesus’ forty days of fasting: a full time of preparation.
str: vv. 1–3: the prologue: the first book, and the forty days of appearances.
vv. 4–5: wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Father, the baptism with the Holy Spirit.
vv. 6–8: the question about the kingdom, and the answer: power from the Spirit and witness to the ends of the earth.
vv. 9–11: he is lifted up, the cloud, the two men in white.
kw: Used in v. 2 and v. 11, and in the Greek Old Testament of Elijah taken up (2 Kings 2:11). The Ascension is not Jesus going away into space; it is his being taken into the glory of God.

“You will be my witnesses” (v. 8). The Greek word later came to mean martyr, one whose witness costs life itself. The verse is the plan of the whole book: Jerusalem (chapters 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–12), and the ends of the earth (13–28).
Not weather but the sign of God’s presence, as on Sinai and at the Transfiguration (Luke 9:34–35). The cloud takes Jesus into the presence of God, out of their sight but not away from them.
vv: appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.
Only Luke gives the number forty. These days were a school: the Risen Lord taught them what the kingdom means, and ate and drank with them (10:41).
“Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?”
The question is not foolish. It is the hope of the prophets. Jesus does not deny that God will fulfil his promises to Israel; he says the times belong to the Father, and he gives them a task for now.
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.
The answer to “when?” is “you”. The kingdom will come through Spirit-filled witness. The ends of the earth include India; the Christians of this land are a fruit of this verse.
as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.
Luke stresses that they saw it. Like Elisha, who received the spirit of Elijah because he saw him taken up, the apostles see the Lord go and will receive his Spirit.
“Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven?

The two men in white recall the two men in dazzling clothes at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4). The Ascension does not invite us to stare at the sky but to turn back to the world with the hope of his return: “will come in the same way”.
ch: The Creed confesses: “He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father. He will come again in glory.” The Catechism teaches that Christ’s Ascension marks the definitive entrance of his humanity into God’s heavenly domain, from where he will come again (CCC 665), and that he precedes us there so that we, his members, may live in the hope of being with him for ever (CCC 666). St Leo the Great preached that the Ascension of Christ is our own uplifting, and that where the glory of the Head has gone, the body is called to follow in hope (in substance). The days of prayer between the Ascension and Pentecost, when the apostles waited with Mary in the upper room (1:14), are the origin of the Church’s novenas.

r.h: Seated at his right hand
set: The Letter to the Ephesians presents itself as Paul’s, written from prison (3:1; 4:1). Many scholars think it was written in Paul’s name by a disciple, near the end of the first century; others hold that Paul wrote it himself. The Church receives it, either way, as the inspired word of God in the Pauline tradition. Some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” in 1:1, and many think it was a circular letter for several churches of Asia.

The letter opens with a great blessing of God for his plan to gather all things in Christ (1:3–14). Our passage is the prayer that follows: that the readers may understand what God has done in raising and enthroning Christ.
str: vv. 17–18a: the prayer for a spirit of wisdom and revelation, and enlightened hearts.
vv. 18b–19: to know three things: the hope, the riches of the inheritance, the greatness of the power.
vv. 20–21: the power at work in Christ: raised, seated at the right hand, above every power and name.
vv. 22–23: all things under his feet; head over all things for the Church, his body, his fullness.
kw: Christ is head of the Church as the source of its life and its Lord. Head and body belong together: the Ascension does not separate Christ from his Church but gives the Church its head in heaven.

The Church is “the fullness of him who fills all in all” (v. 23). The phrase is difficult. It may mean that the Church is filled by Christ, or that the Church in some way completes him as a body completes a head. The Fathers held both senses.

A phrase found only in Ephesians (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12). In 2:6 the letter says that God has already “seated us with him in the heavenly places”. What is said of Christ in our passage is begun in us.
vv: so that, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, you may know what is the hope to which he has called you,
The heart in the Bible is the centre of the person, where we think and decide. Faith gives the heart eyes, so that it can see what the bodily eyes on Ascension day could not: where Christ has gone.
God put this power to work in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places,
An echo of Psalm 110:1, “Sit at my right hand”, the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New. To sit at the right hand of a king is to share his rule.
far above all rule and authority and power and dominion,
These were names for the unseen powers that people feared. Whatever powers there are, Christ is above them all. No fear has the last word over one who belongs to him.
and has made him the head over all things for the church, which is his body,

Christ is head “over all things” not for himself but “for the church”. His lordship is a gift to his people. Psalm 8:6, “you have put all things under their feet”, is quoted in v. 22 and fulfilled in the Son of Man.
ch: The Catechism, explaining Christ seated at the right hand, teaches that Christ is Lord of the cosmos and of history, and head of the Church which is his body, quoting this passage (CCC 668–669). The Second Vatican Council uses the image of head and body to describe the Church (Lumen Gentium 7). St Augustine preached on the Ascension that Christ, though raised above the heavens, still suffers on earth in his members, and that we, though on earth, are already with him in heaven through hope (in substance).

r.h: The Lord worked with them
set: These verses belong to the longer ending of Mark (16:9–20). The two oldest complete Greek manuscripts end the Gospel at 16:8, and many scholars think that the longer ending was added early in the second century, drawing on the other Gospels and Acts. It was known to St Irenaeus, near the end of the second century, and it stands in most manuscripts. The Church receives it as part of the inspired and canonical Gospel; the Council of Trent defined the canon of the books of Scripture with all their parts, and this ending is read in the liturgy.
The Risen Lord appears to the eleven at table, rebukes their unbelief (16:14), and then sends them out.
str: vv. 15–16: the mission: proclaim the good news to the whole creation; faith and baptism.
vv. 17–18: the signs that will accompany those who believe.
v. 19: the Lord Jesus is taken up and sits at the right hand of God.
v. 20: the disciples go out and preach, and the Lord works with them.
kw: Mark begins his book with “the good news of Jesus Christ” (1:1) and ends it with the command to proclaim that good news to the whole creation. The whole Gospel is framed by the word.
Not only to all nations but to all creation. Paul says that creation itself waits with eager longing for the revealing of the children of God (Romans 8:19–21).
The Lord “worked with them” (v. 20). The word gives us “synergy”. The ascended Lord is not absent from the mission; he is its partner and its power.
vv: Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.
The last words of Jesus in Mark are a sending. The disciples who had fled at his arrest (14:50) are now sent to the world.
The one who believes and is baptized will be saved; but the one who does not believe will be condemned.
Faith and baptism go together. The verse speaks of those who hear the good news and refuse it, not of those who never heard it through no fault of their own (see the question below).
they will pick up snakes in their hands, and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not hurt them;

This is a promise of protection in the mission, like Paul unharmed by the viper on Malta (Acts 28:3–6). It is not an invitation to test God by handling snakes on purpose, which Jesus himself refused to do (Matthew 4:7).
So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.
Only here in Mark is Jesus called “the Lord Jesus”, the title of the risen one. “Taken up” echoes Elijah (2 Kings 2:11), and “sat down at the right hand” fulfils Psalm 110:1.
And they went out and proclaimed the good news everywhere, while the Lord worked with them
The Gospel ends not with the disciples looking up but going out. The Ascension begins the time of the Church.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 19 at the start of its teaching on the Ascension (CCC 659). It cites v. 16 when it teaches that faith is necessary for salvation (CCC 161) and that baptism is necessary for salvation for those to whom the Gospel has been proclaimed (CCC 1257). St Leo the Great taught that what was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments (in substance); the Catechism quotes these words (CCC 1115). The Lord who is no longer seen still works with his Church in the word preached and the sacraments celebrated.

qa: If Jesus ascended, is he absent from us now?

No. He said, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20). He is no longer present in the way he was in Galilee, but he is present in a new way: in his word, in the sacraments, above all in the Eucharist, in the Church gathered in his name, and in the poor. The Catechism says that he precedes us into the Father’s glory so that we may live in the hope of being with him (CCC 666).
Was the Ascension a journey upward into the sky?

Luke describes what the apostles saw: he was lifted up and a cloud took him from their sight. The meaning is not a journey through space but Christ’s humanity entering the glory of God. The cloud is the Bible’s sign of God’s presence. “Heaven” here is not a place above the clouds but life with God.
Does Mark 16:16 mean that everyone who is not baptized is lost?

The Church teaches that baptism is necessary for salvation for those who have heard the Gospel and been able to ask for it (CCC 1257). It also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel or the Church, but seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will as their conscience knows it, may attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). God has bound salvation to the sacrament, but he himself is not bound by his sacraments (CCC 1257).
rite: In the Roman Rite the Ascension is a solemnity with its own Preface, which proclaims that Christ ascended not to distance himself from our lowly state but that we, his members, might be confident of following where he, our head, has gone before. In India the Bishops have transferred the solemnity from Thursday to this Sunday so that the faithful may celebrate it together. The Paschal candle remains in the sanctuary until Pentecost, and the Regina Caeli is still prayed. The days from now to Pentecost Sunday, 16 May, are kept as a time of prayer for the Holy Spirit, like the apostles with Mary in the upper room.
study: The angels asked, “why do you stand looking up toward heaven?” Where am I standing still when I should be going out as a witness?
Ephesians prays for “the eyes of your heart enlightened”. What would I like the Lord to help me see more clearly about my hope?
Mark says “the Lord worked with them”. Where have I seen the Lord working with someone who shared the faith?
How can my family pray together for the Holy Spirit in the days before Pentecost?

lead: At Ephesus Paul meets about twelve disciples who have received only John’s baptism and have not even heard of the Holy Spirit. They are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, Paul lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes. In the Gospel the disciples say they now believe, and Jesus warns them that they will be scattered, yet he is not alone, and he has conquered the world. Psalm 68 sings of God who rises and scatters his enemies, father of orphans and protector of widows.

r.h: Did you receive the Holy Spirit?
set: Paul reaches Ephesus, the great city of the province of Asia, on his third journey, as he had promised (18:21). He will stay there more than two years (19:10). Apollos has meanwhile gone to Corinth (19:1), after Priscilla and Aquila taught him the Way more accurately (18:26). The disciples Paul now finds seem to be in a situation like that of Apollos before he was taught.
str: vv. 1–2: Paul meets disciples and asks about the Holy Spirit.
vv. 3–4: John’s baptism of repentance pointed to Jesus.
vv. 5–7: baptism in the name of the Lord Jesus, the laying on of hands, and the gift of the Spirit.
v. 8: three months of bold preaching in the synagogue about the kingdom of God.
kw: Luke calls them disciples, but they seem to have been followers of John the Baptist’s teaching who had not yet received Christian baptism.
John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance that pointed ahead to “the one who was to come” (v. 4). Christian baptism is baptism into Christ, with the gift of the Spirit.
when Paul had laid his hands
The same gesture by which Peter and John gave the Spirit to the baptized of Samaria (8:14–17). The laying on of hands is the ancient gesture of the gift of the Spirit.
vv: “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?” They replied, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.”
They probably knew that John spoke of one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit (Luke 3:16). What they had not heard is that the Spirit had now been given.
John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.
Paul does not belittle John. John’s whole work pointed to Jesus. To follow John faithfully is to come to Christ.
When Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied

This little Pentecost at Ephesus matches the Pentecost at Jerusalem (2:4), the gift at Samaria (8:17) and at Caesarea (10:44–46). In every place the same Spirit is given to the one Church. The “about twelve” may hint at a new beginning, like the twelve tribes and the Twelve.
ch: The Catechism, explaining the sacrament of Confirmation, recalls that the apostles imparted the gift of the Spirit to the newly baptized by the laying on of hands, and cites this passage (CCC 1288). It is one root of the Church’s practice of Confirmation, in which the bishop, successor of the apostles, lays hands on the candidates and anoints them with chrism. Baptism and Confirmation belong together as sacraments of Christian initiation, completed by the Eucharist.

r.h: Take courage; I have conquered the world
set: These are the last words of the farewell discourse before Jesus’ great prayer to the Father in chapter 17. The disciples think they have understood at last. Jesus loves them, but he knows that in a few hours they will run away.
str: vv. 29–30: the disciples: now you speak plainly; now we believe.
vv. 31–32: Jesus: do you now believe? You will be scattered, but I am not alone.
