v. 33: peace in me, persecution in the world, and victory.
kw: The NRSV has “persecution”. The word means pressure, affliction of every kind. Jesus does not promise his disciples a world without trouble.
A word Jesus speaks in the Gospels to the paralysed man, to the woman with the haemorrhage, and to the disciples on the sea: “Take heart, it is I” (Matthew 14:27). Courage comes from his presence.
A perfect tense: the victory is won and remains. John’s first letter echoes it: “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John 5:4).
vv: Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?
Not a rebuke, but a gentle warning. Their faith is real but still untested. It will be tested tonight.
you will be scattered, each one to his home, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone because the Father is with me.

Jesus is not left without the Father even in the hour of desertion. The cry on the Cross in Matthew and Mark, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”, is the opening of Psalm 22, a psalm that ends in trust and praise.
In the world you face persecution. But take courage; I have conquered the world!
The last word of the discourse. The world in John means the world that refuses God, not the world God loves (3:16). His victory is won on the Cross, which looks like defeat.
ch: The Church hears these words above all when Christians suffer for their faith. Many Christians in many lands live this verse today; we pray for them and for those who wrong them. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church, “like a stranger in a foreign land”, presses forward amid the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God (Lumen Gentium 8, quoting St Augustine). Christ’s peace is not the absence of trouble but his presence in the midst of it.

qa: Why were these disciples baptized again, when the Church does not repeat baptism?

They had not received Christian baptism at all, only John’s baptism of repentance. John’s baptism was not the sacrament of baptism into Christ. Christian baptism, once validly received, is never repeated, because it marks the soul with an indelible spiritual sign (CCC 1272).
study: The disciples at Ephesus had not even heard of the Holy Spirit. How often do I think of the Spirit, and what gift of the Spirit do I most need now?
Jesus says, “Take courage; I have conquered the world.” Which trouble in my life do I need to place under his victory?

lead: Paul, on his way to Jerusalem, calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus and speaks to them as a father who knows he will not see his children again. He wants only to finish his course and the ministry received from the Lord Jesus. In the Gospel Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and begins his great prayer: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.” Both readings are farewells, and both look to a work completed. Psalm 68 blesses the Lord who daily bears us up.

r.h: To finish my course
set: Paul is hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (20:16). He does not go up to Ephesus but sends for its elders to come to him at Miletus, a port some distance to the south. This is the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to Christians, to the leaders of a church he founded. It is a farewell speech, like the farewells of Jacob, Moses, Joshua and Samuel, and like Jesus’ own farewell at the Last Supper.
Background. Paul had spent about three years at Ephesus (20:31). It was there, many scholars think, that he wrote 1 Corinthians (1 Corinthians 16:8).
str: vv. 17–18a: the elders of Ephesus come to Miletus.
vv. 18b–21: looking back: humility, tears, trials, teaching in public and from house to house.
vv. 22–24: looking ahead: bound by the Spirit for Jerusalem, prison and persecution awaiting.
vv. 25–27: they will not see him again; he has declared the whole purpose of God.
kw: The leaders of the local church. In v. 28 (tomorrow’s reading) Paul calls the same men episkopoi, overseers. In this early period the two names were used for the same ministry; later the bishop (episkopos) came to be distinguished from the presbyters.
Paul pictures his life as a race to be finished. 2 Timothy 4:7 uses the same word: “I have finished the race”.
“The whole purpose of God” (v. 27): God’s saving plan, all of it. Paul did not choose only the easy or popular parts of the Gospel.
vv: serving the Lord with all humility and with tears,
The word for “serving” is the work of a slave. Paul’s ministry was not a career but service, and his tears show how much the people mattered to him.
teaching you publicly and from house to house,
The early Church gathered in homes. Teaching the faith in the family and the home is as old as the Church.
And now, as a captive to the Spirit, I am on my way to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there,
Literally “bound in the Spirit”. Before he is bound with chains in Jerusalem (21:33), he is already bound by the Spirit. He goes as Jesus went up to Jerusalem, knowing that suffering waits.
But I do not count my life of any value to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus,
Paul does not despise his life; he holds it as less than the mission. The ministry is not his own: he “received” it.
ch: The Church reads this speech as a mirror for every bishop and priest, and for all who serve in the Church. Commentators often call the Miletus speech Paul’s pastoral testament. Paul’s words “the whole purpose of God” remind teachers of the faith to hand on the whole Gospel, the hard parts with the consoling ones. The Second Vatican Council asks priests to be fathers and shepherds to their people, giving their lives as Christ did (Presbyterorum Ordinis 6 and 13, in substance).

r.h: Father, the hour has come
set: John 17 is the longest prayer of Jesus in the Gospels, spoken at the end of the Last Supper before he goes out to the garden. It is often called the “priestly prayer”: Jesus, about to offer himself, prays for himself (vv. 1–5), for his disciples (vv. 6–19), and for all who will believe through their word (vv. 20–26). Today and tomorrow we hear the first two parts.
str: vv. 1–3: glorify your Son; eternal life is to know you.
vv. 4–5: the work finished; the glory before the world existed.
vv. 6–8: the disciples received the word and believed.
vv. 9–11a: I pray for them; they are in the world, I am coming to you.
kw: In John, the Son is glorified on the Cross, where God’s love is shown in full. The “hour” of glory is the hour of the Passion.
Not only life after death but the life of God begun now. Verse 3 defines it: to know the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent.
To know in the biblical sense is not only to have information but to be in a living relationship. Eternal life is friendship with God.
vv: he looked up to heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son so that the Son may glorify you,
Jesus looks up to heaven as he did at the tomb of Lazarus (11:41). The priest at Mass, in the First Eucharistic Prayer, recalls that at the Last Supper Jesus raised his eyes to heaven.
And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.
The faith of Israel in the one God, “the only true God”, is kept whole. Jesus Christ is named with him because the Father is known in the Son whom he sent.
I glorified you on earth by finishing the work that you gave me to do.
He speaks as if the Cross were already done. On the Cross he will say, “It is finished” (19:30), with a verb from the same root.
I am asking on their behalf; I am not asking on behalf of the world,

This does not mean Jesus does not care for the world, which the Father so loved (3:16). Here he prays for the disciples whom he is sending into the world, so that through them the world may believe (17:21).
ch: The Catechism devotes a section to this prayer and says that Christian tradition rightly calls it the “priestly” prayer of Jesus, the prayer of the high priest at the hour of his Passover (CCC 2746–2747). St Cyril of Alexandria, commenting on this chapter, saw Christ here as our high priest and intercessor (in substance). Jesus prays now as he will pray for ever at the Father’s right hand: “he always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25).

qa: What does Jesus mean by “the glory that I had in your presence before the world existed”?

These words (17:5) show that the Son existed with the Father before creation, as the Prologue says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (1:1). The eternal Son became man; in his Passion and Resurrection his humanity enters the glory that he always had as God.
study: Paul says he wants only to finish his course. What is the course God has given me, and what is distracting me from it?
Jesus says eternal life is to know the Father and the Son. What helps me to know God, not only to know about him?

lead: Paul finishes his farewell at Miletus: keep watch over yourselves and the flock, for which God paid with the blood of his own Son; wolves will come; I commend you to God and to the message of his grace. Then he kneels, prays with them, and they weep. In the Gospel Jesus prays for his disciples: protect them, keep them one, sanctify them in the truth. Psalm 68 calls the kingdoms of the earth to sing to God. The Church also remembers today the Roman martyrs Nereus and Achilleus, and the young martyr Pancras.

r.h: Keep watch over the flock
set: This is the second half of Paul’s farewell speech to the elders of Ephesus at Miletus, which began in yesterday’s reading. Having looked back on his own ministry, Paul now hands the care of the church over to them, and warns them of dangers to come.
str: v. 28: keep watch over yourselves and the flock bought with God’s own blood.
vv. 29–31: wolves from outside, distorted teaching from within; be alert.
v. 32: I commend you to God and to the message of his grace.
vv. 33–35: Paul’s example: no greed, work with his own hands, help the weak.
vv. 36–38: prayer, tears and farewell at the ship.
kw: The same men are called “elders” in v. 17. The word gives us “bishop”. Their oversight is not lordship but shepherding: “to shepherd the church of God”.
The task Jesus gave Peter, “Tend my sheep” (John 21:16), and that 1 Peter 5:2 gives to the elders. The model is Christ the Good Shepherd.
God “obtained” the Church with blood. The Church is not a human association but a people God has made his own at great cost.
vv: Keep watch over yourselves and over all the flock, of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God that he obtained with the blood of his own Son.

The shepherd must first watch over himself. Textual note: manuscripts differ between “church of God” and “church of the Lord”, and the Greek can be read “with his own blood” or “with the blood of his own one”, that is, his own Son; the NRSV chooses the second and gives the other in a note. Either way, the Church is bought at the price of Christ’s blood.
I know that after I have gone, savage wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock.
Jesus used the same picture of false prophets in sheep’s clothing (Matthew 7:15). The danger comes from outside and also from within (v. 30).
And now I commend you to God and to the message of his grace,
Paul does not leave them to their own strength. He leaves them to God and to his word, which builds up.
‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’
A saying of Jesus not found in the four Gospels. It shows that sayings of the Lord were remembered and handed on in the early Church beyond what the Gospels record.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the bishops, by divine institution, have succeeded the apostles as shepherds of the Church, and that they are placed by the Holy Spirit as true shepherds of souls (Lumen Gentium 20; Christus Dominus 2). Paul’s self-portrait, working with his own hands and caring for the weak, remains the measure of every pastor. St Augustine, preaching on shepherds, said that for the people he was a bishop, but with them he was a Christian (in substance).

r.h: Sanctify them in the truth
set: We continue the prayer of Jesus at the Last Supper. Having prayed that the Father may glorify him, he now prays for the disciples he is leaving in the world. They are in the world, but they do not belong to it, and they are being sent into it.
str: v. 11b: Holy Father, protect them, that they may be one.
v. 12: I guarded them; none was lost but the one destined to be lost.
vv. 13–16: my joy in them; the world hates them; protect them from the evil one.
vv. 17–19: sanctify them in the truth; I send them; I sanctify myself for them.
kw: The only time in the Gospels Jesus addresses God in this way. The holy Father is asked to make the disciples holy.

To set apart for God and for his service. In the Old Testament priests and sacrifices were consecrated. Jesus consecrates himself (v. 19) as priest and victim, so that the disciples may be consecrated for their mission.
protect them from the evil one
The same petition as the Lord’s Prayer, “deliver us from evil”, which can also be read “from the evil one”. Jesus does not ask that they be taken out of the world, but kept safe in it.
vv: Holy Father, protect them in your name that you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are one.
The unity of the disciples is modelled on the unity of the Father and the Son. It is a gift to be prayed for, not only a task to be organized.
I am not asking you to take them out of the world, but I ask you to protect them from the evil one.
Christian holiness is not escape. The disciples remain in the world, in families, workplaces and villages, and are kept there by God.
Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.
The truth that makes holy is the word of God, and in John the Word is a person (1:1, 14). To be sanctified in the truth is to be made holy by Christ.
And for their sakes I sanctify myself, so that they also may be sanctified in truth.
Jesus consecrates himself as one offers a sacrifice: he gives himself to the Father on the Cross for them. Their holiness flows from his self-offering.
ch: The Church hears this prayer for unity in every work for the unity of Christians. The Second Vatican Council’s decree on ecumenism begins by recalling that Christ prayed that all may be one (Unitatis Redintegratio 2). Pope Benedict XVI, in Jesus of Nazareth, explained that “sanctify” here has a priestly and sacrificial sense: Jesus offers himself, and draws the disciples into his offering (in substance).

qa: What does “the one destined to be lost” mean? Was Judas forced to betray Jesus?

The Greek says “the son of perdition”, a Semitic way of describing one who goes to ruin. It does not mean that God forced Judas. Scripture foresaw the betrayal (Psalm 41:9, quoted in John 13:18), but Judas acted by his own choice. The Church teaches that God’s foreknowledge does not take away human freedom (CCC 600).
rite: Today the Roman calendar offers two optional memorials. Nereus and Achilleus were soldiers in Rome who became Christians and were martyred; the date is uncertain. Pope St Damasus wrote an epitaph for their tomb, saying that they threw down their arms when they believed. Pancras was a youth martyred in Rome, according to tradition at about fourteen years of age, and buried on the Via Aurelia. Like the disciples in today’s Gospel, they lived in the world without belonging to it.
study: Paul tells the elders first to keep watch over themselves. What part of my own life do I need to watch more carefully?
Jesus prays that his disciples may be one. What can I do this week to heal a division in my family, parish or community?

lead: Paul stands before the council in Jerusalem and cries out that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection of the dead. The council divides, the tribune has to rescue him, and that night the Lord stands near him: as he has borne witness in Jerusalem, so he must bear witness in Rome. In the Gospel Jesus prays for those who will believe through the apostles’ word, that is, for us: that we may be one, and be with him where he is. Psalm 16, which Peter quoted on Pentecost of the risen Christ, sings: “you do not give me up to Sheol” (Psalm 16:10). Today is also the optional memorial of Our Lady of Fatima.

r.h: I am on trial concerning the hope of the resurrection
set: Paul was arrested in the Temple when part of the crowd accused him of bringing Gentiles into it (21:27–36). He spoke to the people (22:1–21), and when the tribune was about to have him flogged, Paul revealed that he was a Roman citizen (22:25–29). The tribune, whose name we later learn is Claudius Lysias (23:26), still wants to know the real charge, so he calls the chief priests and the council. In 22:30 “the Jews” means Paul’s accusers in Jerusalem; Paul himself is a Jew and says so proudly. The Lectionary leaves out 23:1–5, where the high priest Ananias has Paul struck on the mouth.

Background. The council (Sanhedrin) was the high court of the Jewish people in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest. Two groups sat in it. The Sadducees, mostly from the priestly families, held to the written Law and did not accept the resurrection (see Luke 20:27). The Pharisees, teachers of the Law close to the ordinary people, believed in the resurrection of the dead, in angels and in spirits, as the Jewish historian Josephus also reports.
str: 22:30: the tribune releases Paul and brings him before the council.
23:6: Paul’s cry: I am a Pharisee, on trial for the hope of the resurrection.
23:7–9: the council divides; some Pharisee scribes defend him.
23:10: the tribune takes him by force into the barracks.
23:11: the Lord stands near him at night: you must bear witness also in Rome.
kw: The Sanhedrin. Jesus, Peter and John, and Stephen had stood before it (Luke 22:66; Acts 4:15; 6:12). Paul now stands where his Lord stood.
For Paul, the hope of Israel and the resurrection belong together (24:15; 26:6–8; 28:20). Christ risen is the first fruits of the resurrection that Israel hoped for (1 Corinthians 15:20).

“So you must bear witness also in Rome.” Luke uses this little word for God’s plan: “Was it not necessary that the Messiah should suffer these things?” (Luke 24:26). Paul’s road to Rome is not an accident of politics but part of God’s design.
vv: “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. I am on trial concerning the hope of the resurrection of the dead.”

Some readers see only a clever move to divide his judges. It is more than that. The resurrection is the centre of Paul’s faith, and it is the point where the Pharisees’ hope and the Gospel meet. Paul calls them “brothers”: he speaks as a son of Israel to his own people.
“We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?”
Some Pharisee scribes take Paul’s side, as the Pharisee Gamaliel had once counselled caution about the apostles (5:34–39). Luke shows that the Pharisees were not simply enemies of the Gospel.
That night the Lord stood near him and said, “Keep up your courage! For just as you have testified for me in Jerusalem, so you must bear witness also in Rome.”

Alone in the barracks, Paul is not alone. The Lord’s word fulfils the plan of Acts 1:8: Jerusalem, then the ends of the earth. On Saturday the Lectionary gives the last verses of Acts, with Paul in Rome.
ch: The Catechism teaches that belief in the resurrection of the dead has been an essential element of the Christian faith from its beginnings, and it quotes Tertullian: the confidence of Christians is the resurrection of the dead (CCC 991). It also recalls that the Pharisees and many of the Lord’s contemporaries hoped for the resurrection, and that Jesus taught it firmly (CCC 993). The Church honours this hope that the Gospel shares with the faith of Israel.

r.h: That they may become completely one
set: This is the last part of the prayer of Jesus at the Last Supper, before he crosses the Kidron valley to the garden (18:1). The prayer has three movements: Jesus prays for himself and his glorification (17:1–5), for the disciples who are with him (17:6–19), and now for all who will come to believe through their word (17:20–26).
str: vv. 20–21: for future believers: one, as the Father and the Son are one, so that the world may believe.
vv. 22–23: the glory given, so that they may be completely one, and the world may know.
v. 24: that they may be with me and see my glory.
vv. 25–26: the world does not know you; I made your name known, so that your love may be in them.
kw: The Greek is neuter, “one thing”, as in “The Father and I are one” (10:30). The unity of believers is modelled on the unity of the Father and the Son, and it comes from it.
Literally “made perfect into one”. Unity is not only given at the start; it grows towards completion.
In v. 24 Jesus does not only ask; he says “I desire”, or “I will”. He speaks as the Son who shares the Father’s will.
vv: I ask not only on behalf of these, but also on behalf of those who will believe in me through their word,
Jesus prays for the Church of every age. Each believer comes to faith “through their word”, the word of the apostles handed on in the Church. Before we prayed, we were prayed for.
that they may all be one. As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.
Unity is not sameness; it is communion, like the communion of the Father and the Son. And it has a purpose: the world’s faith. Division among Christians makes the Gospel harder to believe.
Father, I desire that those also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory,
The goal of the whole prayer is to be with Christ. Heaven is first of all a person and a presence: “with me where I am”.
ch: The Second Vatican Council opens its decree on ecumenism by saying that division among Christians openly contradicts the will of Christ and is a scandal to the world (Unitatis Redintegratio 1), and it quotes this prayer (UR 2). Saint John Paul II took the title of his encyclical on Christian unity, Ut Unum Sint (1995), from v. 21. The Council also saw in v. 21–22 a certain likeness between the union of the divine Persons and the union of God’s children in truth and love (Gaudium et Spes 24). The Catechism teaches that Christ gives his Church the gift of unity, but the Church must always pray and work to keep it and complete it (CCC 820).

qa: Does Jesus’ prayer for unity mean that all Catholics should pray and worship in the same way?

No. The unity of the Church is unity in the one faith, the same sacraments, and the communion of the bishops with the successor of Peter (CCC 815). Within this unity there is a rich variety of rites and traditions. In India the Latin, Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Churches are one Catholic Church, and the Council teaches that such variety does not harm unity but shows it (Orientalium Ecclesiarum 2).
rite: Today the Roman calendar keeps the optional memorial of Our Lady of Fatima. On 13 May 1917, and in the months that followed until October, three shepherd children in Portugal, Lucia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, saw the Blessed Virgin, who asked for prayer, especially the Rosary, for penance and for the conversion of sinners. Francisco and Jacinta were canonised by Pope Francis at Fatima in 2017. The message of Fatima fits today’s Gospel: Mary, who prayed with the apostles, still calls her children to pray for one another and for the world.
study: Jesus prayed for me “through their word”. Who handed on the word of faith to me, and how can I thank God for them?
Where do I see division among Christians or within my own family, and what one step can I take this week for unity?

lead: Today is the Feast of Saint Matthias, Apostle. The first reading tells how he was chosen, in the days between the Ascension and Pentecost, to take the place that Judas had left, so that the Twelve were complete when the Spirit came. The Gospel gives the words that stand behind every apostolic call: “You did not choose me but I chose you.” The choice is Christ’s, and it is a choice of friendship and of fruit that will last.

Psalm 113 sings of the Lord who “raises the poor from the dust”, to make them sit with the princes of his people. Matthias is not mentioned in the Gospels by name and is never mentioned again after this chapter. He is a humble disciple raised by God to sit among the Twelve. In India this year the feast falls between the Ascension (kept last Sunday) and Pentecost, exactly where the reading places it.

r.h: The lot fell on Matthias
set: After the Ascension the apostles returned to Jerusalem and gathered in the upper room, devoting themselves to prayer with the women, with Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers (1:12–14). Before the Spirit comes, Peter rises to act. This is his first act of leadership in Acts. The Lectionary leaves out vv. 18–19, Luke’s account of the death of Judas, which differs in detail from Matthew’s (Matthew 27:3–10); both tell of a field linked with blood.

Background. The Twelve stand for the twelve tribes of Israel. Jesus had promised that they would sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes (Luke 22:30). For the renewed Israel to be complete at Pentecost, the circle of Twelve had to be whole. Casting lots was an accepted way in Israel of leaving a decision to God: “The lot is cast into the lap, but the decision is the Lord’s alone” (Proverbs 16:33). Zechariah was chosen by lot to offer incense in the Temple (Luke 1:9). After Pentecost Acts never again tells of a choice made by lot.
str: vv. 15–17: Peter stands up among about one hundred and twenty; Judas was one of us.
v. 20: two verses of the Psalms: his house desolate; another must take his office.
vv. 21–22: the condition: a companion from John’s baptism to the Ascension, a witness to the resurrection.
v. 23: two are proposed, Joseph Barsabbas (Justus) and Matthias.
vv. 24–25: the prayer to the Lord who knows every heart.
v. 26: the lot falls on Matthias; he is added to the eleven.
¶ The scene moves from Scripture (vv. 16–20), to discernment by the community (vv. 21–23), to prayer (vv. 24–25), and only then to the choice (v. 26).
kw: Judas “was allotted his share” (v. 17, literally “received the lot”) in this ministry, and in v. 26 they “cast lots”. The same word: a share in ministry is always a gift received, never a possession. From klēros comes our word “clergy”.
From Psalm 109:8 in the Greek Old Testament: “Let another take his position of overseer.” The word is related to episkopos, “overseer”, which later became the word for bishop.
The heart of an apostle’s task (v. 22). An apostle is one who was with Jesus, saw him risen, and is sent to tell it.
“Lord, you know everyone’s heart” (v. 24). Luke uses the same word of God in 15:8. The community does its part, and then asks the Lord who sees what they cannot.
vv: In those days Peter stood up among the believers (together the crowd numbered about one hundred twenty persons) and said,

Peter, who denied the Lord three times, now leads his brothers, as Jesus had asked: “strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). St John Chrysostom notes that Peter acts first, as the one entrusted with the flock, yet he does nothing without the whole company (in substance).
for he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.
Judas was truly called and truly one of the Twelve. A call from Christ does not take away human liberty. The verse is sobering, and it is also a reason to pray for all who have been called.
‘Let another take his position of overseer.’
Peter reads two psalms of the suffering just man (Psalm 69:25 and Psalm 109:8) in the light of what happened. The office of an apostle does not die with the one who abandons it; another must take it.
one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.

The one chosen must have walked with Jesus “beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us”. The witness of the apostles is not to an idea but to a person they knew, crucified and risen.
“Lord, you know everyone’s heart. Show us which one of these two you have chosen
They do not ask God to choose; they ask him to show whom he has already chosen. The prayer is addressed to “Lord”, probably the risen Jesus, who chose the Twelve in the first place (1:2).
And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles.

The lot is not chance here but trust: after Scripture, discernment and prayer, the final word is left to God. Joseph Barsabbas, not chosen, remains a disciple. Not being chosen for an office is not being rejected by God.
ch: The Church sees in this scene the first sign of apostolic succession: the apostolic office is meant to continue. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the apostles took care to appoint successors, so that the mission entrusted to them might go on after their death, and that the bishops by divine institution have succeeded to the place of the apostles (Lumen Gentium 20; CCC 861–862). St Clement of Rome, writing to the Corinthians about AD 96, taught that the apostles appointed overseers and deacons and gave instruction that other approved men should succeed them (in substance). Matthias was not one of the first Twelve, but he received the same office and the same witness. The Church today does not choose bishops by lot, but the pattern remains: prayer, discernment, and the conviction that it is the Lord who chooses.

r.h: You did not choose me but I chose you
set: These words come from the farewell discourse at the Last Supper, just after the image of the vine and the branches (15:1–8). Jesus has washed the disciples’ feet (13:1–20) and given them the new commandment (13:34). Now he tells them what kind of bond unites them to him.

Background. In the Old Testament Abraham is called the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8; 2 Chronicles 20:7), and the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, “as one speaks to a friend” (Exodus 33:11). In the courts of the ancient world the “friend of the king” was one who shared the king’s plans. Jesus gives this title to his disciples.
str: vv. 9–11: abide in my love, as I abide in the Father’s; my joy in you.
vv. 12–14: my commandment: love as I have loved; the greatest love is to lay down one’s life.
v. 15: no longer servants but friends.
v. 16: I chose you and appointed you to bear lasting fruit.
v. 17: love one another.
kw: To stay, remain, make one’s home. It runs through the vine passage (15:4–10). Love is not a feeling that comes and goes but a place where we live.
The word is linked to philein, to love. Jesus’ friends are those for whom he lays down his life (v. 13) and to whom he makes known all that he heard from the Father (v. 15).
The same verb as in Luke 6:13, where Jesus chose the Twelve, and in Acts 1:2 and 1:24. In Jesus’ time a disciple usually chose his teacher; here the Teacher chooses his disciples.
Literally “I set, I placed”. The call has a purpose: to go and bear fruit.
vv: As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love.
The love of the Father for the Son is the source; Jesus’ love for us flows from it. We are not asked to produce this love, but to stay in it.
No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends.
Jesus speaks hours before the Cross. Paul goes further: Christ died for us “while we were enemies” (Romans 5:10). Jesus lays down his life for those he makes his friends.
I do not call you servants any longer, because the servant does not know what the master is doing; but I have called you friends,
Being a servant of God is an honour in the Bible (Moses, David, the Servant of Isaiah). Jesus does not cancel service; he lifts it into friendship and shares his heart with those who serve.
You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last,
On the feast of Matthias these words are clear: he was chosen, not self-chosen. Every vocation, to the apostolate, the priesthood, religious life, marriage or any service, begins in Christ’s choice.
I am giving you these commands so that you may love one another.
The passage ends where it began: in love. All the commands come down to one.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus makes charity the new commandment, quoting “As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you; abide in my love” and v. 12 (CCC 1823). It also teaches that the New Law is a law of love that makes us pass from the condition of a servant to that of a friend of Christ, quoting v. 15 (CCC 1972). The Preface of the Apostles praises God who governs his Church through those whom he set over it as shepherds. On this feast the Church thanks God for the apostles, the friends chosen by Christ, and for those who continue their service.

qa: Was choosing Matthias by lot a kind of gambling with God?

No. The apostles did not use the lot to avoid thinking. They first searched the Scriptures, set out the conditions, proposed two worthy men, and prayed. Only then did they cast lots, as Israel had done, trusting that “the decision is the Lord’s alone” (Proverbs 16:33). After the Spirit came at Pentecost, the Church discerned through prayer and the laying on of hands (Acts 6:6; 13:2–3), not by lot.
Why did the Twelve need to be completed, when later no one replaced James after his martyrdom?

Before Pentecost the Twelve had to be whole, as a sign of the renewed Israel with its twelve tribes (Luke 22:30). When James was killed (Acts 12:2), he had remained faithful, and no one was chosen to take his place: the Twelve as a group remain the foundation, as the Book of Revelation shows with the twelve names of the apostles on the foundations of the holy city (Revelation 21:14). Their mission of leading the Church continues through the bishops.
What do we know about Matthias after his election?

The New Testament says nothing more about him. Later traditions differ about where he preached; some name Judea, others regions further away. According to a tradition linked with St Helena, relics believed to be his are venerated at the Abbey of St Matthias in Trier, Germany. What Scripture gives is enough: he was a faithful disciple from the beginning, chosen by the Lord to be a witness of the resurrection.
rite: In the Roman calendar the feast of St Matthias used to be kept on 24 February. In the reform of the calendar after the Second Vatican Council it was moved to 14 May, so that it falls in Eastertide, close to the days between the Ascension and Pentecost when he was chosen. As a feast, the Mass has the Gloria and the Preface of the Apostles, and the vestments are red, the colour of the apostles’ witness. The Collect asks that, through his prayer, we too may be counted among the chosen.
study: Matthias was faithful for years without being noticed, and then was chosen. Where am I asked to be faithful in hidden ways?
The apostles moved from Scripture, to discernment, to prayer, to decision. How do I make important decisions in my life and family?
Jesus says, “I have called you friends.” What would change in my prayer if I spoke to him as a friend?
Joseph Barsabbas was not chosen. How do I respond when I am passed over?

lead: Two books come to their end today. Acts closes with Paul in Rome, under guard, welcoming everyone and proclaiming the kingdom of God “with all boldness and without hindrance”. John’s Gospel closes with Peter told to follow, the beloved disciple who bears witness, and the confession that the world could not hold the books that might be written. Both endings are open: the word goes on. Psalm 11 promises that the upright shall behold God’s face. This evening the Church begins the Solemnity of Pentecost with the Vigil Mass.

r.h: Without hindrance
set: After the storm and shipwreck on Malta (27:1–28:10), Paul and his companions reach Italy and travel to Rome, where the believers come out to meet them (28:13–15). The “we” of v. 16 shows that the narrator travelled with Paul; the Church’s tradition sees in him Luke, Paul’s companion (Colossians 4:14; 2 Timothy 4:11).

Background. Paul lives under a kind of house arrest, chained to a soldier (28:20), while he waits for his case to be heard by the emperor. Acts does not tell the end of his trial or his death. Early Christian tradition, from St Clement of Rome onwards, holds that Paul died a martyr in Rome under Nero. He is honoured with Peter on 29 June, and his tomb is venerated on the Ostian Way.
str: v. 16: arrival in Rome; Paul lives by himself with a soldier guarding him.
vv. 17–20: Paul calls the Jewish leaders of Rome: I have done nothing against our people; I am bound for the hope of Israel.
(vv. 21–29, left out: the discussion and the mixed response.)
vv. 30–31: two whole years, welcoming all, proclaiming the kingdom with boldness and without hindrance.
kw: The hope of the Messiah and of the resurrection. Paul does not preach another religion; he preaches the fulfilment of Israel’s hope in Jesus.
Open, confident speech, the gift for which the apostles prayed in 4:29. It is a fruit of the Spirit.
The very last word of Acts in Greek. Paul is chained, but the word of God is not (2 Timothy 2:9).
vv: “Brothers, though I had done nothing against our people or the customs of our ancestors,

Paul calls the Jewish leaders “brothers” and speaks of “our people”. To the end he is a son of Israel. When v. 19 says that “the Jews objected”, it means his accusers in Jerusalem, and Paul adds that he has no charge to bring against his nation.
it is for the sake of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.”
His chain is not a shame but a witness. He wears it for the hope he shares with his people.
He lived there two whole years at his own expense and welcomed all who came to him,
Even as a prisoner Paul keeps an open house. His lodging becomes a church.
proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.
Acts began with Jesus speaking about the kingdom of God (1:3) and ends with Paul doing the same. The story is unfinished on purpose: it continues in every generation of the Church.
ch: The Church has always seen Rome as the city where Peter and Paul bore their final witness. St Irenaeus, near the end of the second century, spoke of the Church in Rome as founded and established by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul (in substance). The ending of Acts invites each reader to carry on the story: the Spirit who led Paul to Rome now sends the Church to the ends of the earth.

r.h: What is that to you? Follow me!
set: These are the last verses of John’s Gospel. Chapter 21 is an epilogue after the first ending of the Gospel (20:30–31). Jesus has just asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?”, entrusted his sheep to him, and foretold the death by which he would glorify God (21:15–19). Now Peter turns and sees the beloved disciple.
str: vv. 20–21: Peter sees the beloved disciple and asks, “Lord, what about him?”
vv. 22–23: Jesus: what is that to you? Follow me! The rumour that the disciple would not die is corrected.
v. 24: this disciple is the witness who wrote these things.
v. 25: the world could not contain the books.
kw: The first call of the disciples (1:43) and the last word of Jesus to Peter (21:19, 22). The whole Gospel lies between two calls to follow.
The same verb as “abide”. “If it is my will that he remain until I come” (v. 22). The beloved disciple’s way is to remain, Peter’s way is to follow to death.
The Gospel ends with witness: “we know that his testimony is true” (v. 24).
vv: When Peter saw him, he said to Jesus, “Lord, what about him?”
A very human question. Peter has just been told of his own death and wants to know about his friend’s path.
“If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? Follow me!”
Each disciple has his own call. Comparison is a temptation; the answer to it is to follow. Jesus does not tell Peter everything, only what is his to do.
This is the disciple who is testifying to these things and has written them, and we know that his testimony is true.
The “we” is the community that received his witness and vouches for it. The Gospel rests on the testimony of an eyewitness.
if every one of them were written down, I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.
A loving exaggeration. No book can hold all of Jesus. What is written is enough for faith (20:31), but the mystery is always greater.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church firmly holds the historical character of the four Gospels, and that the sacred authors wrote them by selecting some things from the many that had been handed on (Dei Verbum 19). St Augustine saw in Peter and John two lives of the Church: Peter the active life of labour and suffering in this world, John the contemplative life that will be complete in the world to come (in substance). Both belong to the one Church, and both follow the one Lord.

qa: Who wrote the Gospel of John?

The Gospel says that it comes from “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (21:20, 24). From St Irenaeus onwards, the Church’s tradition identifies him with John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve. Many scholars think that the Gospel grew from his testimony and was put in its final form by his disciples, who say “we know that his testimony is true”. Either way, the Church receives it as apostolic, inspired witness.
rite: This evening, in the Roman Rite, the Vigil Mass of Pentecost may be celebrated. The Roman Missal provides an extended form of this Vigil, with several Old Testament readings (Genesis 11 on Babel, Exodus 19 on Sinai, Ezekiel 37 on the dry bones, Joel 3 on the Spirit poured out), so that the Church may wait in prayer like the apostles with Mary in the upper room.
study: Jesus says to Peter, “what is that to you? Follow me!” In what area of my life do I compare myself with others instead of following?
Paul welcomed “all who came to him” even in chains. Who comes to my door, and how do I welcome them?

lead: Today the fifty days of Easter reach their fulfilment. The three readings tell of the one gift of the Spirit from three sides. Acts tells the event: on the Jewish feast of Pentecost a sound like wind, tongues as of fire, and the apostles speaking so that people of many nations hear God’s deeds of power in their own languages. Paul tells its meaning in the Church: one Spirit, many gifts, one body. John goes back to Easter evening, when the risen Lord breathed on the disciples, gave them his peace, sent them, and gave them power to forgive sins.

Psalm 104 gives the prayer of the day: “When you send forth your spirit, they are created; and you renew the face of the ground” (Psalm 104:30). Before the Gospel the Church sings the Sequence, Veni, Sancte Spiritus, “Come, Holy Spirit”, which is obligatory today. It is usually attributed to Stephen Langton, archbishop of Canterbury in the early thirteenth century, and is often called the Golden Sequence.

r.h: All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit
set: The disciples, about one hundred and twenty, with Mary the mother of Jesus, have been praying together in Jerusalem since the Ascension (1:14–15). Jesus had told them to wait for “the promise of the Father” and power from on high (1:4, 8). Now the promise is fulfilled.

Background. Pentecost, “the fiftieth day”, is the Greek name of the Jewish Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), kept seven weeks after Passover (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). It was one of the three pilgrim feasts, when many Jews came to Jerusalem, and it offered God the first fruits of the wheat harvest. In Jewish tradition the feast also came to be linked with the giving of the Law at Sinai, where the Lord came down in fire, with thunder and the sound of a trumpet (Exodus 19:16–19). Many readers also hear in Pentecost the undoing of Babel, where human pride led to the confusion of languages (Genesis 11:1–9).
str: v. 1: the day of Pentecost; all together in one place.
vv. 2–3: a sound from heaven like a violent wind; tongues as of fire rest on each.
v. 4: all are filled with the Holy Spirit and speak in other languages.
vv. 5–8: devout Jews from every nation hear, each in his own language.
vv. 9–11: the list of peoples; all hear of God’s deeds of power.
kw: The fiftieth day after Passover. For the Church it is the fiftieth day after Easter, the completion of the Paschal mystery.

Luke uses pnoē for the “wind” (v. 2) and pneuma for the Spirit (v. 4). In Hebrew the one word rûaḥ means wind, breath and spirit. The wind is a sign of the Spirit who cannot be seen but whose power is felt (John 3:8).
The same word means tongues of fire (v. 3) and the languages spoken (v. 4). The fire is not destructive but a gift of speech: the Spirit gives a tongue to proclaim.
The mighty works of God, the great acts of salvation (in Latin, magnalia Dei). This is what the apostles proclaim: not themselves, but what God has done in Christ.
vv: When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place.
“Had come” translates a word meaning “was being fulfilled”. Luke presents the day as the fulfilment of a time of waiting. They are together: the Spirit comes on a praying community.
And suddenly from heaven there came a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
The sound comes “from heaven”, from God. The house is filled, as the glory of the Lord once filled the tabernacle and the Temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11).
Divided tongues, as of fire, appeared among them, and a tongue rested on each of them.
Luke uses “as of” and “like”: he describes what cannot be fully described. The fire is divided and rests on each. The one Spirit is given to each person.
All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit gave them ability.
“All of them”, not only the apostles. The gift of speech comes “as the Spirit gave”: it is not their skill but his gift.
And how is it that we hear, each of us, in our own native language?
God speaks to each people in its own language. The Gospel can be at home in every culture, in Malayalam, Tamil, Hindi and English as much as in Greek or Latin.
ch: The Catechism teaches that on the day of Pentecost, when the seven weeks of Easter had come to an end, Christ’s Passover is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (CCC 731), and that on that day the Holy Trinity is fully revealed (CCC 732). The Council teaches that the Spirit was sent on the day of Pentecost to sanctify the Church continually (Lumen Gentium 4; CCC 767). St Irenaeus wrote that the Spirit brought the scattered peoples into unity and offered to the Father the first fruits of all nations, so that in all languages they praised God with one accord (in substance). The Preface of Pentecost praises the Spirit who, as the Church came to birth, brought together the many languages of the earth in the confession of one faith.

r.h: In the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body
set: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, probably around AD 54–55, to the community he had founded in Corinth. The Corinthians were rich in spiritual gifts but divided (1:10–12). Some prized the more striking gifts, especially speaking in tongues, and looked down on others. In chapters 12–14 Paul teaches them about the gifts of the Spirit, and at the centre he places love (chapter 13).
str: v. 3b: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit.
vv. 4–6: varieties of gifts, services and activities; the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God.
v. 7: to each for the common good.
v. 12: one body, many members; so it is with Christ.
v. 13: baptized in one Spirit into one body; all made to drink of one Spirit.
kw: Gifts of grace (from charis, grace). They are given, not earned, and they are given for others.

Paul uses three words for the gifts and links them with the Spirit, the Lord and God. Many see here an early witness to the faith in the Trinity: one God, Father, Son and Spirit, at work in the Church.
What builds up all. The test of a gift is whether it serves the body.
For Paul the Church is not like a body only in a loose way; it is the body of Christ (12:27). Each member belongs to the others.
vv: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit.
“Jesus is Lord” was the first Christian confession of faith (Romans 10:9). To say it truly, with the heart, is already the work of the Spirit. The first gift of the Spirit is faith in Jesus.
Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit;
Unity is not uniformity. The one Spirit makes variety, and holds it together.
To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
“To each”: no believer is without a gift. “For the common good”: no gift is for oneself alone.
For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.
Paul does not say “so it is with the Church” but “so it is with Christ”. Christ and his members form one body.
For in the one Spirit we were all baptized into one body … and we were all made to drink of one Spirit.
Baptism makes us one body in the Spirit. To “drink” the Spirit recalls the living water Jesus promised (John 7:37–39). Many Fathers also heard in it an allusion to the sacraments that follow baptism.
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on the Holy Spirit with v. 3: no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit (CCC 683). It teaches that charisms, extraordinary or simple and humble, are graces of the Spirit oriented to building up the Church and the good of all, and that they must be received with gratitude and discerned by the Church’s pastors (CCC 799–801). The unity of the body does not do away with the diversity of its members (CCC 791; Lumen Gentium 7). St Augustine told the newly baptized at Pentecost that if they are the body of Christ and his members, their own mystery is placed on the Lord’s table: “be what you see, and receive what you are” (in substance).

r.h: Receive the Holy Spirit
set: It is the evening of Easter day. That morning Mary Magdalene found the tomb empty and met the risen Lord (20:1–18). The disciples are behind locked doors. John’s “for fear of the Jews” means fear of the authorities who had handed Jesus over; the disciples themselves, like Jesus, were Jews.

Background. In the creation story God formed the man from the dust and “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). In Ezekiel’s vision the prophet is told to call the breath to come upon the slain, “that they may live” (Ezekiel 37:9). Jesus’ breath on the disciples recalls both: a new creation, and the dead raised to life.
str: v. 19: evening, locked doors; Jesus stands among them: “Peace be with you.”
v. 20: he shows his hands and side; they rejoice.
v. 21: peace again; as the Father sent me, so I send you.
v. 22: he breathes on them: “Receive the Holy Spirit.”
v. 23: the power to forgive and to retain sins.
kw: The Hebrew shalom: wholeness, salvation, the gift of the Messiah. Jesus had promised, “Peace I leave with you” (14:27). Now he gives it, risen, to men who had abandoned him.
Found only here in the New Testament. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7, when God breathes life into the first man. Easter evening is the new creation.
“As the Father has sent me, so I send you.” The mission of the Church is the continuation of the mission of the Son. The word “apostle” means one who is sent.
Literally “hold fast”. The disciples receive power both to loose and to hold, a power that Christ gives, not one they possess of themselves.
vv: the doors of the house where the disciples had met were locked for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.”
Locked doors cannot keep him out, and fear cannot keep him away. The first word of the risen Lord to the disciples is not a reproach but peace.
Then the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord.
Jesus had promised, “I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice” (16:22). He shows his wounds: the risen one is the crucified one.
“Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, so I send you.”
The disciples are sent as Jesus was sent: with the same love, and to the same world, ready to suffer for it.
When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.
In John the gift of the Spirit flows from the risen and glorified Jesus (7:39). Easter and Pentecost belong together as one mystery.
If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained.”
The first fruit of the Spirit given at Easter is forgiveness. Christ entrusts to his apostles the ministry of reconciliation.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it teaches about the sacrament of Penance: on the evening of Easter the Lord Jesus showed himself to his apostles and gave them the Holy Spirit and the power to forgive sins (CCC 1485). The Council of Trent taught that these words refer to the power of forgiving and retaining sins in the sacrament of Penance (Session 14). The peace of Christ, the mission of the Church, and the forgiveness of sins are all gifts of the one Spirit.

qa: Did the disciples receive the Spirit at Easter (John) or at Pentecost (Acts)?

Both writers tell of the one gift of the risen Lord. John shows that the Spirit flows from Christ crucified and risen, on Easter evening itself. Luke shows the public outpouring on the fiftieth day, when the Church is made manifest to the nations. St John Chrysostom explained that on Easter evening the Lord gave a grace for the forgiveness of sins, and at Pentecost the fullness of power for the mission (in substance). The Church celebrates the fifty days as one feast, completed today.
Was the miracle of Pentecost in the speaking or in the hearing?

Luke says both: the apostles “began to speak in other languages” (2:4), and each one “heard them speaking in the native language of each” (2:6). St Gregory of Nazianzus, in a sermon on Pentecost, discussed this question and thought the miracle was chiefly in the speaking (in substance). What matters is the meaning: the Gospel is for all peoples, each in its own tongue.
Does the Holy Spirit still give his gifts today?

Yes. The Council teaches that the Spirit distributes special graces among the faithful of every rank, simple as well as extraordinary, for the renewal and building up of the Church (Lumen Gentium 12). Every Christian receives the Spirit in Baptism and Confirmation. The gifts are to be received with gratitude, used in charity, and discerned by the pastors of the Church (CCC 800–801).
rite: Pentecost is a solemnity, and with it the Easter season ends. The vestments are red. The Sequence, Veni, Sancte Spiritus, is obligatory today. After Pentecost the Paschal candle is taken from the sanctuary and kept near the baptismal font, to be lit at baptisms and funerals. The Regina Caeli gives way again to the Angelus. Tomorrow Ordinary Time resumes, beginning with the memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church: the Mother who prayed with the apostles for the Spirit is honoured on the day after his coming.
study: The Spirit came on a community at prayer. How can my family or parish pray together for the Spirit?
Paul says, “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.” What gift has God given me for others?
The risen Lord’s first word was “Peace”. Where do I need to receive his peace, and where can I bring it?
The first gift of the Spirit in John is forgiveness. When did I last receive the sacrament of Reconciliation?

lead: On the day after Pentecost the Roman Rite honours the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church. The readings take us to two moments: the garden, where after the first sin God promises enmity between the serpent and the woman and her offspring, and the Cross, where Jesus gives his mother to the beloved disciple and the disciple to his mother. The Lectionary also allows Acts 1:12–14, where the apostles pray “together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” before Pentecost.
Psalm 87 sings of Zion, the city of God, as the mother of the peoples: “This one was born there.” The Church, the new Jerusalem, is our mother, and Mary is the mother of the Church.

r.h: I will put enmity between you and the woman
set: The man and the woman have eaten from the tree, their eyes have been opened, and they have hidden themselves from God among the trees of the garden (3:1–8). Now God comes to find them. The Lectionary leaves out vv. 16–19, the consequences for the woman and the man, and adds v. 20, where the man names his wife Eve.

Background. This is part of the second account of creation (2:4b–3:24). It tells in the language of images a real event at the beginning of human history, the first sin, as the Catechism teaches (CCC 390). The serpent is the figure of the tempter, whom the Book of Revelation calls “that ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan” (Revelation 12:9).
str: vv. 9–10: “Where are you?” I was afraid and hid.
vv. 11–13: God questions; the man blames the woman, the woman blames the serpent.
v. 14: the curse on the serpent.
v. 15: enmity between the serpent and the woman, his offspring and hers.
v. 20: Eve, mother of all living.
kw: God’s first question to fallen man. Not because God does not know, but to call the man out of hiding. It is the question of a Father seeking his child.
A lasting hostility. God himself puts it: the human race will not be left in friendship with evil.
It can mean descendants in general or one descendant. Christian tradition reads it of Christ, the offspring of the woman who defeats the serpent.
The name sounds like the Hebrew word for “living”. Eve is “the mother of all living”. The Fathers called Mary the new Eve, mother of all who live in Christ.
vv: But the Lord God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
Sin makes us hide; God comes looking. The whole of salvation history begins with this search.
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.”
The first fruit of sin is broken relationship: the man blames the woman, and even God who gave her. The unity of the first couple is wounded.
I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.

Even before the punishment of the man and woman, God speaks a promise. The Hebrew says “he” (or “it”), meaning the offspring; the old Latin Vulgate read “she”, and so many paintings show Mary crushing the serpent. The Church’s faith does not rest on that reading: the victory belongs to Christ, and Mary shares in it as his mother, wholly on his side against the serpent.
The man named his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
After the sentence of death, the man gives his wife a name of life. Hope is not lost.
ch: The Catechism calls Genesis 3:15 the “Protoevangelium”, the first announcement of the Messiah and Redeemer, of a battle between the serpent and the Woman, and of the final victory of a descendant of hers. Many Fathers and Doctors of the Church see the Woman as Mary, the mother of Christ, the new Eve (CCC 410–411). St Irenaeus taught that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was loosed by Mary’s obedience; what the virgin Eve bound by unbelief, the Virgin Mary loosed by faith. The Council quotes him (Lumen Gentium 56), and it recalls that the promise of victory over the serpent foreshadows Mary (Lumen Gentium 55). Blessed Pius IX cited this verse in defining the Immaculate Conception in 1854.

r.h: Woman, here is your son. Here is your mother
set: Jesus has been crucified, and the soldiers have divided his clothes (19:23–24). Only John tells that the mother of Jesus stood near the Cross. In John’s Gospel she appears only twice, at Cana (2:1–12) and at Calvary, and she is never named; she is “the mother of Jesus”. At Cana Jesus said to her, “Woman, ... My hour has not yet come” (2:4). Now the hour has come (13:1).
str: v. 25: the women near the Cross.
vv. 26–27: “Woman, here is your son.” “Here is your mother.” The disciple takes her into his own home.
vv. 28–30: “I am thirsty”; the sour wine; “It is finished”; he gives up his spirit.
vv. 31–33: the legs of Jesus are not broken.
v. 34: the soldier pierces his side; blood and water flow.
kw: A respectful form of address, used also at Cana (2:4). It recalls “the woman” of Genesis 3:15 and the mother of the new humanity.
Literally “into his own”: among the things that were his. The disciple welcomes Mary into his life as a treasured gift.
Accomplished, brought to its goal. The work the Father gave the Son is complete (17:4).
Literally “handed over the spirit”. He dies, and his death already looks towards the gift of the Spirit to the Church.
vv: standing near the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
They stand. Mary does not flee. She who said “Here am I, the servant of the Lord” (Luke 1:38) remains faithful at the hour of the Cross.
When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing beside her, he said to his mother, “Woman, here is your son.”
The beloved disciple is not named. The Church sees in him every disciple whom Jesus loves. From the Cross Jesus gives his mother a new motherhood.
Then he said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.
This is more than a son providing for his widowed mother. It is the gift of the hour: Mary becomes mother of the disciples, and the disciple receives her.
When Jesus had received the wine, he said, “It is finished.” Then he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
He bows his head first, then hands over his spirit: in John he lays down his life of his own accord (10:18).
Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.

John insists that he saw it (19:35). The Fathers saw in the blood and water the sacraments of the Eucharist and Baptism, and the Church born from the side of Christ, as Eve was formed from the side of Adam.
ch: The Council teaches that “from the side of Christ as he slept the sleep of death upon the Cross there came forth the wondrous sacrament of the whole Church” (Sacrosanctum Concilium 5; CCC 766). Lumen Gentium says that Mary, standing at the Cross, was given by the dying Jesus as mother to his disciple (Lumen Gentium 58; CCC 964), and, quoting St Augustine, that she is truly mother of the members of Christ, because she cooperated by her love so that the faithful might be born in the Church (Lumen Gentium 53; CCC 963). St Paul VI proclaimed Mary Mother of the Church on 21 November 1964, at the Council. Saint John Paul II wrote that the disciple’s taking Mary “into his own” is the model for every Christian who entrusts himself to her (Redemptoris Mater 45).

qa: Why does Jesus call his mother “Woman”?

It is not cold or disrespectful. In Greek it was a courteous form of address. In John it has a deeper meaning: Mary at Cana and at the Cross is “the woman” whose offspring defeats the serpent (Genesis 3:15), the new Eve, the mother of the new people of God. Jesus speaks to her not only as her son, but as Redeemer, giving her a mission.
Does calling Mary “Mother of the Church” put her in the place of Christ?

No. The Council teaches that there is one mediator, Christ, and that Mary’s maternal role does not obscure or diminish his unique mediation but shows its power; it flows from his merits and depends on them entirely (Lumen Gentium 60). Mary is the first and most excellent member of the Church, and at the same time its mother (Lumen Gentium 53). She always leads us to her Son: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).
rite: In 2018 Pope Francis inscribed this memorial in the General Roman Calendar for the Monday after Pentecost (decree Ecclesia Mater of the Congregation for Divine Worship, 11 February 2018), so that the Church, born at Pentecost, might honour the Mother who prayed with the apostles for the Spirit. It is an obligatory memorial. With it the Church in the Roman Rite resumes Ordinary Time, in the seventh week this year; the vestments are white for the memorial.
study: God asks Adam, “Where are you?” Where am I hiding from God now?
Mary stood near the Cross. Whose suffering am I called to stand near, without running away?
The disciple took Mary into his own home. What place does Mary have in my home and my family prayer?

lead: Ordinary Time has resumed. Sirach warns the one who comes to serve the Lord to be ready for testing, and encourages him: look at the generations of old; has anyone trusted in the Lord and been disappointed? In the Gospel Jesus again tells the disciples that he will be handed over, killed and rise, and they argue about who is the greatest. He places a child among them. Psalm 37 answers: “Commit your life to the Lord, and he will help you.”

r.h: Prepare yourself for testing
set: Jesus ben Sira was a teacher of wisdom in Jerusalem around 180 BC. His grandson translated the book into Greek in Egypt some time after 132 BC, as he explains in his prologue. Large parts of the Hebrew text have been found in modern times, in the Cairo Genizah and at Masada. The book is one of the deuterocanonical books, received by the Catholic Church as Scripture. Its Latin name, Ecclesiasticus, “the church book”, comes from its wide use in teaching the faithful.
Chapter 1 praised wisdom and the fear of the Lord. Chapter 2 turns to the one who sets out to live it: the road will include trials.
str: vv. 1–6: whoever serves the Lord will be tested: be steadfast, cling to him, accept, trust; gold is tested in fire.
vv. 7–9: three calls: “You who fear the Lord”: wait for his mercy, trust him, hope for good things.
vv. 10–11: look at the generations of old; the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
kw: The trial that proves and purifies faith. It is not the same as temptation to sin. The same Greek word can mean both, and the context decides.
Not terror but reverent love that keeps one faithful; “the beginning of wisdom” (Sirach 1:14). The phrase returns again and again in today’s passage.
God’s steadfast, faithful kindness. Verse 11 echoes the great self-revelation of God to Moses: “merciful and gracious” (Exodus 34:6).
vv: My child, when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing.
A teacher speaks to his pupil as a father to a son. He does not promise an easy road; he prepares the young believer for it.
For gold is tested in the fire, and those found acceptable, in the furnace of humiliation.
The same image appears in Wisdom 3:6 and 1 Peter 1:7. Fire does not destroy gold; it purifies it.
has anyone trusted in the Lord and been disappointed?
An appeal to memory. Israel’s history, with Abraham, Joseph, Moses and David, shows that God does not abandon those who trust him.
For the Lord is compassionate and merciful; he forgives sins and saves in time of distress.
The last word is not the trial but the mercy of God.
ch: The Catechism, explaining the petition “lead us not into temptation”, teaches that the Holy Spirit helps us to discern between trials, which are necessary for the growth of the inner person, and temptation, which leads to sin and death (CCC 2847). The New Testament takes up Sirach’s teaching: “whenever you face trials of any kind, consider it nothing but joy” (James 1:2), because tested faith produces endurance.

r.h: Whoever wants to be first must be last
set: This is the second of Jesus’ three predictions of his Passion in Mark (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34). It comes after the Transfiguration and the healing of the boy with a spirit (9:2–29). Jesus is on the way that leads to Jerusalem. Each prediction is followed by the disciples’ misunderstanding and by teaching about the way of discipleship.
str: vv. 30–32: passing through Galilee in secret; the prediction; they do not understand and are afraid to ask.
vv. 33–34: in the house at Capernaum: “What were you arguing about?” Silence.
v. 35: the first must be last of all and servant of all.
vv. 36–37: the child in his arms; whoever welcomes a child welcomes me.
kw: is to be betrayed, handed over
A present tense: it is already happening. The same verb is used of Judas handing Jesus over, and of God giving up his Son for us (Romans 8:32).
One who waits at table. Jesus will say that he came “not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).
In that world a child had no status and no rights. To welcome a child was to welcome one who could give nothing in return.
vv: But they did not understand what he was saying and were afraid to ask him.
They are afraid of the answer. Sometimes we too prefer not to ask what following Jesus will cost.
But they were silent, for on the way they had argued with one another who was the greatest.
While Jesus speaks of the Cross, they speak of rank. Their silence shows that they know they were wrong.
He sat down, called the twelve, and said to them, “Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.”
He sits, as a teacher sits to teach. He does not forbid the desire to be first; he shows the way to it: service.
“Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes not me but the one who sent me.”
Jesus identifies himself with the least. To welcome the little one is to welcome Christ, and in him the Father.
ch: The Council teaches that the office the Lord gave to the pastors of his people is a true service, which Scripture significantly calls diakonia, ministry (Lumen Gentium 24). Since St Gregory the Great the Pope has called himself “servant of the servants of God”. The Church hears in this Gospel a call to every Christian, and above all to those who lead, to measure greatness by service, and to welcome the smallest: children, the poor, the sick and the unborn.

qa: Does Jesus forbid ambition?

No. He does not condemn the wish to be first; he turns it upside down. The way to true greatness is to be “servant of all”. Using our gifts well and aiming high are good when they serve others and not our own pride.
rite: Today is the optional memorial of St John I, Pope and Martyr. He was Bishop of Rome from 523 to 526. The Arian king Theodoric, ruler of Italy, sent him to Constantinople to plead with the emperor Justin on behalf of the Arians in the East. When he returned, the king, suspecting him, held him in prison at Ravenna, where he died in 526. He is honoured as a martyr. Sirach’s word fits him: “when you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing.”
study: Sirach asks, “has anyone trusted in the Lord and been disappointed?” When has God been faithful to me in a time of trial?
Who is the “child” in my life, the person with no status, whom Jesus asks me to welcome in his name?

lead: Ben Sira paints Wisdom as a mother and teacher who tests her children before she trusts them, and then shows them her secrets. In the Gospel John wants to stop a stranger who drives out demons in Jesus’ name, and Jesus will not allow it. Psalm 119 sings of the great peace of those who love God’s law. Both readings teach the same lesson: Wisdom, and the name of Jesus, are larger than the circle we draw around ourselves.

r.h: Whoever loves her loves life
set: The Book of Sirach is the work of a Jerusalem teacher, Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach (50:27), written in Hebrew about 180 BC. His grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt some fifty years later, as his prologue tells. The Church received the book in Greek; large parts of the Hebrew were found again from 1896 onward, first in the Cairo Genizah and later at Masada and Qumran. Latin Christians called it Ecclesiasticus, the “church book”, because it was so widely used for teaching. It is one of the deuterocanonical books, received by the Catholic Church as Scripture.

In chapter 4 the teacher has just spoken of care for the poor and the orphan (4:1–10). Now he turns to Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman who brings up children, a figure he will develop at length in chapter 24.
str: vv. 11–13: Wisdom teaches and helps; those who love her are filled with joy.
vv. 14–16: to serve her is to serve the Holy One; the faithful inherit her.
vv. 17–18: first the hard road of her discipline, then gladness and her secrets.
v. 19: the warning: those who stray are left to their ruin.
kw: In Sirach wisdom is practical skill for living rightly before God, and also something greater: a gift that comes from the Lord (1:1) and is close to him, here pictured as a person.
Training, the bringing up of a child, with its corrections (v. 17). Ben Sira knows that learning costs something. Hebrews 12:5–11 uses the same word for the Lord’s discipline of his children.

“Those who serve her minister to the Holy One” (v. 14). In the Greek Old Testament this verb is used for the service of priests, and our word “liturgy” comes from it. To live wisely is itself a kind of worship.
vv: Wisdom teaches her children and gives help to those who seek her.
The NRSV follows the Hebrew, “teaches”. The Greek, which the Malayalam follows, says that Wisdom “exalts” her sons. Both are true of her: she instructs, and she lifts up.
Whoever loves her loves life, and those who seek her from early morning are filled with joy.
Seeking “from early morning” is the language of eager love (compare Proverbs 8:17). Wisdom is not a subject one studies once; she is sought every day.
For at first she will walk with them on tortuous paths;
An honest word. The road to wisdom has bends and trials. She tests before she trusts, and then she “will come straight back to them again and gladden them” (v. 18).
ch: Christians have long heard in these portraits of Wisdom an echo of Christ, whom Paul calls “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). The Catechism names wisdom first among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831). The road Ben Sira describes, discipline first and then joy, is the road of every disciple who keeps faith through dark times.

r.h: Whoever is not against us is for us
set: We are in the house at Capernaum (9:33). Jesus has just foretold his passion for the second time (9:31), and the disciples have argued on the road about who is the greatest. He has set a child among them and said that whoever welcomes such a child in his name welcomes him (9:37). The word “name” sets John speaking; this is the only place in Mark where John speaks on his own.

Background. Numbers 11:26–29 tells a similar story. Two elders, Eldad and Medad, prophesied in the camp although they had not gone out to the tent, and Joshua asked Moses to stop them. Moses answered that he wished all the Lord’s people were prophets.
str: v. 38: John reports that they tried to stop an outsider.
v. 39: Jesus says, do not stop him: no one who does a deed of power in my name will soon speak evil of me.
v. 40: the principle: whoever is not against us is for us.
kw: In the Bible the name stands for the person and his power. The man drives out demons “in your name”, by calling on Jesus himself. The word runs through these verses: in my name (v. 37), in your name (v. 38), in my name (v. 39).
“He was not following us,” says John, not “you”. The disciples measure by belonging to their group; Jesus measures by a person’s relation to himself.
Mark’s usual word for Jesus’ miracles. Even outside the circle of the Twelve, the power at work is his.
vv: Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.
Only a little earlier the disciples themselves could not drive out a demon (9:18, 28). The man they want to stop is doing what they had failed to do.
Do not stop him;
Jesus is not jealous for the size of his group but glad for the good done in his name.
Whoever is not against us is for us.

In Matthew 12:30 Jesus says, “Whoever is not with me is against me.” The sayings do not contradict each other. One warns our own hearts: no one can stay neutral before Jesus. The other teaches generosity toward others who do good in his name.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the one Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, while many elements of sanctification and of truth are found outside her visible structure (Lumen Gentium 8). Catholics are asked to acknowledge gladly the truly Christian gifts found among other Christians (Unitatis Redintegratio 4). The disciple rejoices wherever the name of Jesus brings healing, and does not confuse loyalty to Christ with suspicion of everyone outside one’s own circle.

qa: Does this mean it does not matter which Church one belongs to?

No. Jesus is not saying that every group is the same, but that good done in his name comes from him and must not be opposed out of rivalry. The Church teaches that the fullness of the means of salvation is found in the Catholic Church (Unitatis Redintegratio 3). At the same time she honours what is truly of Christ in other Christians, and prays and works for unity.
study: Where do I find it hard to rejoice in good done by people outside my own group or parish?
Ben Sira says Wisdom tests before she trusts. What hard stretch of my road might be her discipline?

lead: Ben Sira warns against false confidence: trust in wealth, trust in one’s own strength, and trust that mercy can be put off until later. In the Gospel Jesus speaks just as plainly: a cup of water given to his disciples will be rewarded, and whatever leads us or others into sin must be cut away. Psalm 1 sets the two ways side by side, the tree planted by streams of water and the chaff that the wind drives away.

r.h: Do not delay to turn back to the Lord
set: After his chapters on wisdom and humility, Ben Sira gives a string of short commands, nearly all beginning “Do not”. Each warns against a confidence that is false: in money, in one’s own strength, in God’s patience, in God’s mercy taken for granted.

Ben Sira writes before the clear revelation of the life to come. When he speaks of punishment and of the day of calamity, he thinks first of judgment within this life. Later revelation opens the fuller horizon, but his call to conversion stands.
str: vv. 1–2: do not trust wealth or your own strength.
vv. 3–4: do not say that no one can call you to account.
vv. 5–6: do not presume on forgiveness.
vv. 7–8: turn back today; dishonest wealth will not save you.
kw: The Greek word behind “turn back” (v. 7) is the Bible’s great word for conversion: to turn around and come home to God.
God’s patience (v. 4) is real, but it is given so that we may repent, not so that we may go on sinning. Paul says the same in Romans 2:4.
“Both mercy and wrath are with him” (v. 6). Ben Sira does not deny mercy; he warns against using it as an excuse.
vv: Do not say, “I sinned, yet what has happened to me?” for the Lord is slow to anger.
Because nothing happened at once, the sinner thinks nothing will happen. God’s delay is not approval; it is an invitation.
Do not be so confident of forgiveness that you add sin to sin.
This is presumption: counting on forgiveness while refusing conversion.
Do not delay to turn back to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day;
St Augustine remembered how, before his conversion, he kept saying “tomorrow, tomorrow” (Confessions, Book 8, in substance). Ben Sira’s word is for today.
ch: The Catechism names presumption as a sin against hope: a person either trusts in his own powers to be saved, or presumes on God’s mercy, hoping to be forgiven without conversion (CCC 2092). The Church never preaches less mercy. She preaches mercy received now, in repentance and in the sacrament of Penance, not stored up for later.

r.h: Have salt in yourselves
