set: The teaching in the house at Capernaum goes on. Mark gathers sayings linked partly by key words: “name” (vv. 38–41), “stumble” (vv. 42–47), “fire” and “salt” (vv. 48–50). Such links helped the first Christians to remember Jesus’ words.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, which repeat verse 48, and add at verse 49 the words “and every sacrifice will be salted with salt” (compare Leviticus 2:13). The NRSV follows the oldest manuscripts and leaves them out, so its numbering skips. Malayalam Bibles number these verses differently.
str: v. 41: a cup of water given because you belong to Christ will be rewarded.
v. 42: woe to whoever makes a little one stumble.
vv. 43–48: hand, foot, eye: cut away what leads to sin.
vv. 49–50: fire and salt; be at peace with one another.
kw: From skandalon, a trap or stumbling block: to make someone fall away from faith or into sin. The verb comes four times in these verses.

Gehenna, the valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, once a place where children were burned in sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). It became the name for the final punishment. Verse 48 takes its words from the last verse of Isaiah (66:24).
Literally a “donkey millstone”, the heavy stone turned by an animal, not the small hand mill of a household.
vv: whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you bear the name of Christ will by no means lose the reward.
The smallest kindness shown to a disciple for Christ’s sake is not forgotten. The outsider of the previous verses is still in view.
If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off;
This is the strong speech of a prophet, not an order to harm the body. What must be cut away is the habit, the attachment, the occasion that leads us into sin.
Salt is good; but if salt has lost its saltiness, how can you season it? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.
Salt preserves and gives taste, and in Leviticus 2:13 it seasons every offering. The section that began with an argument about who was greatest (9:34) ends with peace.
ch: The Church has never read these words as permission to injure the body: the Catechism teaches that mutilation is against the moral law except for strictly therapeutic reasons (CCC 2297). But she takes their seriousness to heart. The Catechism recalls Jesus’ words on Gehenna and the unquenchable fire when it teaches about hell, and calls that teaching an urgent call to conversion (CCC 1034, 1036). Scandal, leading another into sin, is grave, the more so when it harms the weak and the young (CCC 2284–2285).

rite: Today is the optional memorial of St Bernardine of Siena (1380–1444), the Franciscan preacher who carried through the towns of Italy a tablet painted with the letters IHS, the first letters of the name of Jesus in Greek, and spread devotion to the Holy Name. The Gospel fits him well: it begins with a cup of water given “because you bear the name of Christ”.
study: What false confidence (money, strength, or “tomorrow”) keeps me from turning to the Lord today?
What in my life, or in what I let others see, could become a stumbling block for the little ones?

lead: Ben Sira writes about friendship: friends of convenience disappear in hard times, but a faithful friend is a sturdy shelter and life-saving medicine. In the Gospel Pharisees test Jesus with a question about divorce, and he takes them back to the beginning of creation: what God has joined together, let no one separate. Psalm 119 asks for guidance in the way of God’s commands, the way that makes both friendship and marriage last.

r.h: Faithful friends are a sturdy shelter
set: Ben Sira lived in a society where friendship mattered greatly for safety, trade and good name. He brings the subject under the fear of the Lord: true friendship grows out of faithfulness to God.
His teaching moves in three steps: gentle speech wins friends; test them before you trust them; a faithful friend is beyond price.
str: vv. 5–7: be friendly to many, take few as advisers, and test them.
vv. 8–13: friends who leave you in time of trouble.
vv. 14–16: the faithful friend: shelter, treasure, medicine.
v. 17: those who fear the Lord find friends like themselves.
kw: The phrase comes three times in vv. 14–16, like a refrain. Pistos means faithful, trustworthy, a word the Bible also uses of God’s own faithfulness.
A covering, a protection from sun and storm. A faithful friend gives what a house gives.
Literally “medicine of life” (v. 16). St Ignatius of Antioch later called the Eucharist the “medicine of immortality” (Letter to the Ephesians 20).
vv: When you gain friends, gain them through testing, and do not trust them hastily.
Not suspicion but prudence. Trust grows with time and proof.
Faithful friends are a sturdy shelter: whoever finds one has found a treasure.
“Finds”: a faithful friend is a gift received, not a possession we make.
Faithful friends are life-saving medicine; and those who fear the Lord will find them.
The secret of friendship is not cleverness but the fear of the Lord. Those who are faithful to God become faithful friends, and draw such friends to themselves (v. 17).
ch: Jesus lifts friendship to its height: “I have called you friends” (John 15:15), and “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (John 15:13). The Catechism teaches that the virtue of chastity blossoms in friendship, and that friendship is a great good for all (CCC 2347). St Aelred of Rievaulx wrote a whole book, On Spiritual Friendship, about friends who love one another in Christ.

r.h: What God has joined together
set: Jesus leaves Galilee for the last time and goes toward Jerusalem, into Judea and the land beyond the Jordan. The land beyond the Jordan was ruled by Herod Antipas, who had imprisoned John the Baptist for speaking against his marriage to his brother’s wife and later had him beheaded (6:17–28). A question about divorce there was a dangerous one.

Background. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 takes for granted that a man may give his wife a certificate of divorce if he finds “something objectionable” in her. Jewish teachers of the time disputed what this meant: the school of Shammai allowed divorce only for serious sexual wrongdoing, the school of Hillel for much lesser reasons. The certificate at least protected the woman, who could then marry again.
str: v. 1: the journey to Judea and beyond the Jordan.
vv. 2–4: the test question and the law of Moses.
vv. 5–9: the concession of Moses and God’s plan from the beginning.
vv. 10–12: in the house the teaching is made plain to the disciples.
kw: The law allowed divorce because of human hardness, not because it was God’s plan. Jesus reaches behind the concession to the will of the Creator.
The written bill of divorce of Deuteronomy 24:1.
Literally, to yoke together. God himself joins husband and wife; the bond of marriage is his work.
vv: Because of your hardness of heart he wrote this commandment for you.
Moses put up with what he could not cure. Jesus comes to heal the hard heart itself, and so he can restore the beginning.
But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’
Jesus quotes Genesis 1:27 and then 2:24. He answers a question about the law by going back to creation.
Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
The word is for everyone: spouses, families, society and the state. No human authority can undo what God has bound.
and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.
Jewish law of the time did not usually let a wife divorce her husband, but Roman law did. Mark spells out the teaching for Christians living in the Roman world.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus unequivocally taught the original meaning of the union of man and woman as the Creator willed it from the beginning, and that the permission given by Moses was a concession to hardness of heart (CCC 1614). Christ gives the strength to live marriage in its original meaning (CCC 1615). The Church cannot recognise a new union as valid while the first valid marriage stands (CCC 1650), yet she asks priests and the whole community to show attentive care to those in this situation, so that they do not think of themselves as separated from the Church (CCC 1651).

qa: Is an annulment a Catholic divorce?

No. A divorce claims to end a marriage. A declaration of nullity is the Church’s judgment, after careful examination, that a valid marriage never came into being, for example because true consent was lacking (CCC 1629). The Church also allows a couple to separate when living together becomes impossible or dangerous, though they remain husband and wife before God (CCC 1649).
study: Who has been a faithful friend to me in a time of trouble, and to whom am I such a friend?
How can our family or parish stand by married couples who are struggling to stay together?

lead: Ben Sira looks at the human being as God made us: taken from the earth and returning to it, yet made in God’s image, given eyes, ears and a mind, and taught the law of life. In the Gospel Jesus is indignant when his disciples turn children away, and says that the kingdom belongs to such as these. Psalm 103 holds both truths together: we are dust and our days are like grass, but the Lord’s kindness is everlasting to those who fear him.

r.h: He made them in his own image
set: This is Ben Sira’s meditation on Genesis 1–3 and on Sinai. He moves from creation (vv. 1–10) to covenant and law (vv. 11–14), and ends with God, who sees all our ways (v. 15).

Textual note. Sirach has come down in a shorter and a longer Greek form, and the Latin Vulgate follows a longer one. Some lines found only in the longer forms are not printed in the NRSV, which is why it has no verse 5. The Malayalam text numbers these verses differently.
str: vv. 1–4: made from earth, given a fixed number of days and authority over the earth.
vv. 6–10: the gifts of senses, mind and knowledge, so that they may praise God.
vv. 11–14: the law of life and an eternal covenant.
v. 15: their ways are always known to him.
kw: “He made them in his own image” (v. 3), from Genesis 1:27. For Ben Sira the image shows itself in authority over creation and in the power to know God and praise him.
The law is given not as a burden but as the way of life (compare Deuteronomy 30:15–20).
The covenant of Sinai, where “their eyes saw his glorious majesty” (v. 13).
vv: The Lord created human beings out of earth, and makes them return to it again.
Genesis 2:7 and 3:19 in one line. Humility and dignity together: we are dust, but dust shaped by God’s hands.
He filled them with knowledge and understanding, and showed them good and evil.
Ben Sira speaks of knowing good and evil as God’s gift: the moral sense, conscience, by which we can choose the good.
He said to them, “Beware of all evil.” And he gave commandment to each of them concerning the neighbor.
The two tables of the law in brief: turn from evil before God, and do right by your neighbour.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the human person, created in the image of God, is able to know and love the Creator and was appointed by him master of all earthly creatures, to rule them and use them while glorifying God (Gaudium et Spes 12). The Catechism adds that by reason and will the person is ordered to his true good (CCC 1704–1705). Ben Sira’s praise of human dignity is one root of the Church’s defence of every human life.

r.h: Let the little children come to me
set: Right after the teaching on marriage comes a scene with children. In the ancient world children were loved, but they had little standing in public life. The disciples, perhaps wanting to protect their busy Master, scold those who bring them.
Mark alone among the Gospels says that Jesus was indignant, and that he took the children in his arms.
str: v. 13: children are brought; the disciples rebuke the people.
v. 14: Jesus is indignant: let them come.
v. 15: receive the kingdom as a little child.
v. 16: he embraces and blesses them.
kw: A strong word of anger. In the Gospels it is used of Jesus only here. What angers him is that the little ones are kept from him.
A small child. The point is not innocence but dependence: a child receives what it cannot earn.
Only Mark uses this word, here and in 9:36. Jesus does not only teach about children; he holds them.
vv: Let the little children come to me; do not stop them; for it is to such as these that the kingdom of God belongs.
“Do not stop them”: the same Greek words as “Do not stop him” in 9:39. Twice in two chapters the disciples try to keep people away, and twice Jesus opens the door.
whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will never enter it.
The kingdom is first received, then entered. We come with open hands.
And he took them up in his arms, laid his hands on them, and blessed them.
Three gestures: embrace, laying on of hands, blessing. Parents who bring their children to the priest for a blessing continue this scene.
ch: The Catechism recalls this Gospel when it speaks of the hope of salvation for children who die without Baptism, trusting in Jesus’ tenderness toward children (CCC 1261). The Church baptises infants because the grace of salvation is a pure gift (CCC 1250). And she teaches that to become a child in relation to God is the condition for entering the kingdom (CCC 526).

qa: Why does the Church baptise babies who cannot yet believe?

Because Baptism is God’s gift before it is our achievement. Children are born into a fallen world and need new life in Christ, and the Church has baptised them from very early times, with parents and godparents promising to bring them up in the faith (CCC 1250–1255).
rite: Today is the optional memorial of St Rita of Cascia (about 1381–1457). Married young in Umbria, she bore her husband’s harsh temper with patience and prayer; when he was murdered she forgave those who killed him and prayed that her sons would not take revenge. Widowed and alone, she entered the Augustinian convent at Cascia. Wives, mothers and families in difficulty turn to her as a patron of impossible causes.
study: What in me needs to become more like a child before God: more trusting, more ready to receive?
Ben Sira says God gave each of us a commandment concerning the neighbour. Who is the neighbour I find hardest to do right by?

lead: On the Sunday after Pentecost the Church gathers all that she has celebrated, from Christmas to the coming of the Spirit, into one act of worship of the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The readings do not give a definition. They tell a story: God who chose a people and spoke to them out of the fire (Deuteronomy), God who makes us his children by the Spirit who cries “Abba” in us (Romans), and the Risen Son who sends his disciples to baptise in the one name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew).

Psalm 33 sings of the Lord whose word made the heavens and whose eye is on those who fear him. Moses tells Israel that there is no other God. Jesus does not change that faith; he reveals the inner life of the one God and draws us into it.

r.h: There is no other
set: Deuteronomy presents itself as the farewell speeches of Moses on the plains of Moab, before Israel enters the promised land. Chapter 4 closes the first speech. Moses has warned Israel against making any image of God, since at Horeb they saw no form but only heard a voice (4:12, 15). Now he asks them to look back over all history.

Background. Many scholars think Deuteronomy reached its final form over a long time, and that this chapter speaks also to Israel in exile, when the pull of the gods of the nations was strong. Its message is for every age: the Lord alone is God.
str: v. 32: ask about all the ages since creation: has anything so great ever happened?
v. 33: a people heard God’s voice out of the fire and lived.
v. 34: God took a nation for himself out of Egypt.
v. 39: therefore know and take to heart: the Lord is God, there is no other.
v. 40: keep his commandments, for your good and your children’s.
kw: The phrase closes verses 35 and 39. It is one of the clearest confessions of the one God in the whole Torah, close to the Shema of 6:4.
Not only to know a fact but to recognise it and accept it with the whole self; hence “take to heart”.
The plagues and tests in Egypt (v. 34). God makes himself known through his mighty deeds.
vv: has anything so great as this ever happened or has its like ever been heard of?
Moses invites Israel to compare. Faith rests on what God has done in history.
Has any people ever heard the voice of a god speaking out of a fire, as you have heard, and lived?
At Sinai the people feared that they would die (5:24–26). God speaks, and those who hear him live.
So acknowledge today and take to heart that the Lord is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.
“Today”: each generation must make this confession its own.
Keep his statutes and his commandments, which I am commanding you today for your own well-being
Obedience flows from knowing who God is, and it is for our good.
ch: The Church reads this passage on Trinity Sunday to remind us that faith in the Trinity is faith in one God. The Catechism begins its teaching on God with Israel’s confession of the only God, “Hear, O Israel”, and with the prophet’s word that there is no other (CCC 200–201). The Trinity is not three gods, but the one God revealed as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, a mystery hidden in God that could never be known unless he revealed it (CCC 237).

r.h: Abba! Father!
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome, a community he had not founded, around AD 57, probably from Corinth. Chapter 8 is the summit of the letter. Paul has shown that all have sinned and that God justifies by grace through faith in Christ; now he describes the new life of those who live by the Spirit.
Just before our passage he contrasts life according to the flesh and life according to the Spirit (8:5–13). Now he says what the Spirit makes us: children of God.
str: v. 14: those led by the Spirit are children of God.
v. 15: not a spirit of slavery but of adoption; we cry “Abba”.
v. 16: the Spirit bears witness with our spirit.
v. 17: children, and so heirs with Christ, if we suffer with him.
kw: A legal word in the Roman world: one who was adopted received the full rights of a son and became an heir. Christ is Son by nature; we become children by grace.
The Aramaic word for “father”, used within the family. The Greek-speaking Church kept it untranslated (also in Mark 14:36 and Galatians 4:6) because it was Jesus’ own word in prayer.
The Spirit joins his witness to ours. Our confidence that we are God’s children does not rest on our feelings but on the Spirit’s testimony, received in faith and prayer.
vv: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God.
To be led is to let another guide. The Christian life is not first our effort but the Spirit’s leading, to which we respond.
you have received a spirit of adoption. When we cry, “Abba! Father!”
The Trinity appears in prayer itself: in the Spirit we call God “Father” with the very word of the Son.
it is that very Spirit bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God,
This is the confidence of hope, not a certainty we hold in our own hands (CCC 2005). We trust the Spirit more than our moods.
and if children, then heirs, heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ
The inheritance is God himself. The way to it is the way of the Son: suffering with him so as to be glorified with him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that grace makes us adopted children of God and partakers of the divine nature (CCC 1996), and that God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying “Abba! Father!” (CCC 683, quoting Galatians 4:6). All Christian prayer is shaped by this. We dare to call God “Father” because the Son has revealed him and the Spirit makes us his children (CCC 2780–2782).

r.h: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
set: These are the last verses of Matthew’s Gospel. The women at the tomb were told that the Risen Jesus would go ahead of the disciples to Galilee (28:7, 10). Now the eleven go to the mountain. In Matthew mountains are places of revelation: the temptation (4:8), the great sermon (5:1), the Transfiguration (17:1).

Matthew wrote for a community of Jewish and Gentile believers, probably in the later decades of the first century. The Gospel that began with “Emmanuel”, God is with us (1:23), ends with “I am with you always.”
str: v. 16: the eleven go to the mountain in Galilee.
v. 17: worship and doubt.
v. 18: all authority in heaven and on earth.
vv. 19–20a: go, make disciples, baptise, teach.
v. 20b: I am with you always.
kw: Better, to hesitate, to be of two minds. The same verb describes Peter sinking in the water (14:31). Jesus does not wait for perfect faith; he comes near and speaks.
The one main command; going, baptising and teaching serve it. A disciple is a learner who follows a master for life.
Not “names” but one name. Baptism plunges the believer into the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and makes him or her belong to God.
vv: When they saw him, they worshiped him; but some doubted.
An honest Gospel: even at the end, worship and hesitation stand side by side among the disciples.
All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.
An echo of Daniel 7:14, where the Son of Man receives dominion. The kingdoms the devil offered on another mountain (4:8–9) the Father has given to the obedient Son.
baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
The early Christian instruction called the Didache, probably from the late first or early second century, already gives this same formula for Baptism (Didache 7).
And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
Not a memory but a presence, every day until the end.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christians are baptised “in the name” and not “in the names” of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, for there is only one God (CCC 233). It quotes St Gregory of Nazianzus, who promised the catechumens of Constantinople to give them the profession of faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as the companion and guardian of their whole life (CCC 256, in substance). The missionary mandate of these verses is the source of the Church’s mission to all nations (CCC 849).

qa: Is the Trinity in the Old Testament?

Not as a clear teaching. The Old Testament reveals the one God, as today’s first reading insists. The Fathers saw hints in it, such as God’s Word, his Spirit and his Wisdom, but the inner mystery of God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit was revealed by the coming of the Son and the sending of the Spirit (CCC 237).
How can three be one?

The Church does not say that three gods are one god, nor that one person wears three masks. She confesses one God in three distinct Persons, each of them fully God, distinct by their relations to one another (CCC 253–255). It is a mystery beyond reason, not against it, and it tells us that God is love, a communion, not a solitude.
Why did some of the disciples doubt, even then?
Matthew does not hide it. Faith in the Risen Lord grew through meeting him, hearing him and being sent by him. Our hesitations do not stop Jesus from coming near and entrusting us with his mission.
rite: The Solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity is kept on the Sunday after Pentecost; Pope John XXII extended it to the whole Latin Church in 1334. Its Preface sings that with the Only Begotten Son and the Holy Spirit the Father is “one God, one Lord: not in the unity of a single person, but in a Trinity of one substance”. Every Mass begins and ends in the name of the Trinity, and before the Our Father the priest invites us to “dare to say” it, with the boldness of children. In India, Corpus Christi is kept next Sunday, 30 May. At home, a family might make the Sign of the Cross and pray the Glory Be slowly together today, remembering their Baptism.
study: Moses asks Israel to look back over all history. Where can I look back and see God’s hand in my own story?
When I pray “Father”, do I remember that it is the Spirit who prays in me with the word of the Son?
Jesus sent the eleven even though some doubted. What mission is he entrusting to me in spite of my hesitations?
How can our family make the Sign of the Cross a real act of faith and not only a habit?

lead: Ben Sira calls sinners home: the Lord grants a way back to those who repent, and his mercy to those who turn to him is great. In the Gospel a man runs to Jesus, kneels and asks about eternal life; Jesus looks at him with love and asks for everything, and the man goes away grieving. Psalm 32 sings the joy of the one whose sin is forgiven.

r.h: Turn back to the Lord
set: After his hymn to God the Creator who gave the covenant (17:1–14), Ben Sira says that God sees all human deeds (17:15–23). Then comes a call to repentance. The Lectionary numbers these verses 17:20–24, following a different division of the text; the NRSV numbers them 17:24–29.

Ben Sira, like the older psalms, pictures the dead in Hades as unable to praise God (vv. 27–28). Later revelation, in the Book of Wisdom, in 2 Maccabees, and above all in Christ’s resurrection, opens the hope of life with God after death.
str: v. 24: God grants a way back to those who repent.
vv. 25–26: turn back, pray, hate what he abhors.
vv. 27–28: the living praise God; the dead do not.
v. 29: how great is the Lord’s mercy.
kw: A change of mind and heart. Ben Sira uses it for those to whom God grants a way back (v. 24).
A road home. Repentance is not only sorrow; it is a way that God himself opens.
The Greek name for Sheol, the shadowy place of the dead in the older books of the Old Testament.
vv: Yet to those who repent he grants a return, and he encourages those who are losing hope.
God does not only accept the sinner who comes back; he strengthens the discouraged so that they can come back.
Who will sing praises to the Most High in Hades in place of the living who give thanks?
Compare Psalm 6:5 and Isaiah 38:18. The point is urgent: now is the time to turn and give praise.
How great is the mercy of the Lord, and his forgiveness for those who return to him!
The passage ends not with fear but with wonder at mercy.
ch: The Catechism describes conversion as the movement of a contrite heart, drawn and moved by grace to respond to the merciful love of God who loved us first (CCC 1428). The way back that Ben Sira praises is opened fully in Christ and given in the sacrament of Penance, which the Fathers called “the second plank” of salvation after the shipwreck of sin (CCC 1446).

r.h: Jesus, looking at him, loved him
set: Jesus is “setting out on a journey”, on the road to Jerusalem. Matthew calls the man young (19:20) and Luke calls him a ruler (18:18); Mark says only that he ran and knelt, and that he had many possessions.
Many in Israel, as in other cultures, saw wealth as a sign of God’s blessing (compare Deuteronomy 28:1–14). That is why the disciples are so astonished at Jesus’ words.
str: vv. 17–18: the question, and Jesus’ answer: no one is good but God.
vv. 19–20: the commandments, kept since youth.
vv. 21–22: Jesus looks, loves and calls; the man goes away grieving.
vv. 23–27: the camel and the needle; for God all things are possible.
kw: “Jesus, looking at him, loved him” (v. 21). Only Mark records this look of love. The hard call that follows comes from love.
“You lack one thing.” Not more rules, but the one thing: to follow Jesus with an undivided heart.

The largest animal of the land, through the smallest opening. Attempts to soften the image, such as a small gate called “the needle’s eye” or a rope instead of a camel, have no good ancient support. Jesus means what is humanly impossible.
vv: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?
He asks what he must do. Jesus will show him that eternal life is received from God and lived in following him.
Jesus, looking at him, loved him and said, “You lack one thing; go, sell what you own, and give the money to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”
The call is personal. Jesus does not ask every disciple to sell everything, but he asks every disciple to put nothing before him.
For mortals it is impossible, but not for God; for God all things are possible.
An echo of Genesis 18:14, “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” Salvation is God’s work, and by his grace we respond.
ch: The Catechism presents this meeting as a model of the moral life: keeping the commandments is the first step, and following Christ is its fullness (CCC 2052–2053). St John Paul II built the first chapter of his encyclical Veritatis Splendor on this dialogue as Matthew tells it. Clement of Alexandria wrote a work on this passage, “Who is the rich man that is saved?”, teaching that what must be given up is above all the rule of riches over the heart (in substance).

qa: When Jesus says “No one is good but God alone”, is he denying that he is God?

No. He is leading the man to think about what he has said. If only God is good, and the man rightly calls Jesus good, then he stands before more than a teacher. The same Jesus then asks the man to leave everything and follow him, something only God could rightly ask.
study: What possession, habit or security would I find hardest to give up if Jesus asked me today?
Ben Sira says God encourages those who are losing hope. Whom can I encourage to come back to the Lord this week?

lead: Ben Sira, a teacher who loved the Temple, tells his students what makes an offering pleasing to God: keeping the commandments, kindness, almsgiving, a cheerful face, and honest hands. In the Gospel Peter, still thinking of the rich man who went away sad, reminds Jesus that the disciples have left everything. Jesus answers with a promise: a hundredfold now, with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come. Psalm 50 joins the two: the sacrifice God wants is thanksgiving from a heart that walks in his way.

r.h: Give as he has given to you
set: Jesus Ben Sira taught in Jerusalem about 180 years before Christ, while the Temple sacrifices were still offered every day. He was no enemy of worship. Later in the book he describes the high priest Simon at the altar with deep admiration (chapter 50). But he wants his students to understand what gives the offering its worth.

The passage moves from the inward to the outward. First, a life of obedience and mercy is itself a sacrifice (vv. 1–5). Then, because that is so, the outward offering must not be neglected either: no one should come before the Lord empty-handed (v. 6). The Lectionary stops at v. 12; the further verses in our Bible add the reason: God repays, and he cannot be bribed.
str: vv. 1–5: obedience, kindness, almsgiving and turning from wrong are offerings in their own right.
vv. 6–9: do not come empty-handed; the gift of the righteous is accepted and remembered.
vv. 10–13: give generously and gladly, as God has given to you, for he repays sevenfold.
vv. 14–15: no bribe, no dishonest sacrifice; the Lord is a judge without partiality.
kw: The general word for what is brought to God. Ben Sira lines up the Temple offerings one by one (the offering of well-being, choice flour, the thank offering, atonement) and sets a moral act beside each.
From eleos, mercy. Alms are mercy made visible. Ben Sira, like Tobit, gives almsgiving a high place among the works pleasing to God (compare Tobit 12:8–9).

Ben Sira’s favourite name for God (vv. 8, 12). The one who receives our gifts is above all things and needs nothing from us; that is why he cannot be bribed (v. 14), and why a poor man’s small gift is not despised.
vv: The one who keeps the law makes many offerings;
Ben Sira does not set the law against worship. A faithful life is already worship, and it gives the Temple gift its truth.
and one who gives alms sacrifices a thank offering.
The thank offering was the sacrifice of a grateful heart. To share one’s goods with the poor is to thank God for what he has given.
Do not appear before the Lord empty-handed,
The inward attitude does not cancel the outward gift. Israel had been told the same at its pilgrim feasts (Deuteronomy 16:16). The body, the hands and the purse also belong to God.
Give to the Most High as he has given to you, and as generously as you can afford.
The measure of our giving is God’s giving to us. The verse is realistic too: “as you can afford”. God does not ask for what we do not have; he asks for a generous heart within what we do have.
ch: The Church keeps Ben Sira’s balance. Inward conversion comes first, but it is shown in visible acts. The Catechism notes that Scripture and the Fathers insist above all on three forms of penance, fasting, prayer and almsgiving (CCC 1434). St Paul writes in the same spirit that “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). At every Mass the gifts are brought to the altar together with the offering of the faithful for the Church and the poor. Ben Sira would recognise the scene: an honest gift, given with gladness, from a life that keeps the commandments.

r.h: A hundredfold, with persecutions
set: The scene continues directly from the meeting with the rich man, who went away grieving because he had many possessions (10:17–22), and from Jesus’ words about how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom (10:23–27). Peter speaks for the Twelve. They have done what the rich man could not.
str: v. 28: Peter: “we have left everything”.
vv. 29–30: the promise: a hundredfold now, with persecutions, and eternal life in the age to come.
v. 31: the first will be last and the last first.
kw: An image of overflowing abundance, like the seed that yields a hundredfold in the parable (4:8, 20).
Only Mark adds “with persecutions” to the list of rewards. His readers, many think in Rome after the persecution under Nero, knew what this meant.
Jewish teaching spoke of “this age” and “the age to come”. Jesus speaks of both: a reward now and eternal life then.
vv: Look, we have left everything and followed you.
It is partly true and partly a question. Peter wants to know whether it was worth it. Jesus does not scold him.
who will not receive a hundredfold now in this age … houses, brothers and sisters, mothers and children, and fields, with persecutions

The new family is the community of disciples, where those who left home find many homes, many brothers and sisters, many mothers. Notice that “fathers” is not repeated in the list. Some commentators see here a hint that in the new family there is one Father, God (compare Matthew 23:9).
But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.
A warning to Peter as well. Those who have left everything must not now count themselves first. The kingdom is always a gift.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and to renounce all they have for his sake and that of the Gospel (CCC 2544). The Church has seen in this promise the life of priests and religious who leave home and family, and also the life of every Christian who puts Christ first. The hundredfold is not a business deal. It is the experience of those who find, in the Church, a family wider than blood, and in the midst of trials a joy that does not depend on what they own.

qa: Does this promise mean that those who give up things will become rich?

No. Jesus speaks of houses and fields in the new family of disciples, shared and given, and he adds “with persecutions”. The promise is about a life made rich in relationships and in God, not about money. The prosperity idea, that faith brings wealth, does not fit a Gospel that has just sent the rich man away sad.
rite: Today three optional memorials may be kept. St Bede the Venerable (died 735), a monk of Jarrow in northern England, wrote commentaries on Scripture, including Mark and Luke, and the Ecclesiastical History of the English People; Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church. St Gregory VII, pope from 1073 to 1085, worked to end the control of rulers over the Church’s appointments and died in exile at Salerno. St Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi (died 1607) was a Carmelite nun of Florence, known for her love of the Eucharist and her prayer for the renewal of the Church. Each of them left something for Christ, and each found the hundredfold.
study: What have I given to God this week from what he has given me? Did I give it gladly?
Where have I found, in the Church, the brothers, sisters and mothers Jesus promises?

lead: Ben Sira prays for his people under foreign powers: have mercy, gather the tribes of Jacob, and let all the nations know that there is no God but you. In the Gospel Jesus walks ahead of his frightened disciples on the road to Jerusalem and tells them for the third time what will happen there. James and John ask for the best seats in his glory. Jesus answers that greatness means service, because the Son of Man came to give his life a ransom for many. On the memorial of St Philip Neri, Psalm 79 asks the Lord to show us the light of his kindness.

r.h: Let them know that there is no God but you
set: This is Ben Sira’s great prayer of petition for the whole people, rather than for the teacher himself. It asks God to act against the foreign nations that oppress Israel, to gather the scattered tribes, and to fill Zion with his glory. Many scholars think it reflects the hard years under the Seleucid kings of Syria in the second century before Christ. Some think it was added to the book in the time of the Maccabees; others hold that Ben Sira wrote it himself.

The verse numbers differ from Bible to Bible here, because the ancient manuscripts arrange this part of the book differently. The Lectionary leaves out the verses that ask most strongly for the destruction of enemies (vv. 6–12 in our numbering).
str: v. 1: “Have mercy upon us, O God of all.”
vv. 4–5: as Israel has shown God’s holiness to the nations, may the nations come to know him too.
vv. 13–17: gather the tribes of Jacob; have mercy on Israel, your firstborn, and on Jerusalem.
vv. 18–22: fill Zion with your glory, fulfil the prophecies, hear the prayer of your servants.
kw: The prayer opens with a cry for mercy, the same word as in “Kyrie eleison”. The whole petition rests on God’s faithful love, not on Israel’s merit.
God had called Israel “my firstborn son” when he sent Moses to Pharaoh (Exodus 4:22). The title means a special love and a special task, not that the other nations are unloved.
Jerusalem is named as the city of God’s sanctuary, the place of his dwelling. The prayer longs for the Temple to be filled with his glory.
vv: Have mercy upon us, O God of all,
He is “God of all”, not only of Israel. That is why the prayer can end by hoping that all on earth will know him.
As you have used us to show your holiness to them, so use them to show your glory to us.
A striking request. When Israel was punished, the nations saw God’s holiness. Now Ben Sira asks that when Israel is restored, the nations themselves will see God’s glory.
Then they will know, as we have known, that there is no God but you, O Lord.
The deepest hope of the prayer is not revenge but knowledge of God. The nations are to know him as Israel knows him.
all who are on the earth will know that you are the Lord, the God of the ages.
The prayer ends where it began: with God over all. Christians hear in this the mission of the Church to all nations, the work of the God who keeps his promises to Israel.
ch: The Church prays part of this text as a canticle in the Liturgy of the Hours, a prayer of the whole people of God. She also reads it in the light of Christ: the gathering of the scattered children of God (John 11:52) and the knowledge of God among the nations. The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church, the new people of God, draws sustenance from the root of that good olive tree onto which the Gentiles have been grafted (Nostra Aetate 4). God’s gifts and call to Israel are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). So the Christian reader prays with Ben Sira for Israel, and for all nations, that the God of the ages be known.

r.h: Not to be served but to serve
set: Mark’s central section (8:27–10:52) is a journey “on the way” to Jerusalem. Three times Jesus foretells his passion (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34), and three times the disciples fail to understand: Peter rebukes him, the disciples argue about who is the greatest, and now James and John ask for places of honour. Each time Jesus teaches about following him.
This third prediction is the most detailed. It names the handing over to the Gentiles, the mocking, the spitting and the flogging, all of which happen in the Passion narrative.
str: vv. 32–34: Jesus walks ahead; the third prediction of the passion.
vv. 35–40: the request of James and John; the cup and the baptism.
vv. 41–45: the anger of the ten; greatness as service; the Son of Man gives his life a ransom for many.
kw: In the Old Testament the cup often stands for a destiny given by God, sometimes the cup of his wrath (Isaiah 51:17). In Gethsemane Jesus will pray, “remove this cup from me” (14:36).
Two words in rising strength (vv. 43–44). The great one must be a servant; the first must be the slave of all. From diakonos comes the word deacon.
The price paid to release a captive or a slave. Jesus gives his own life to release the many from sin. “Many” recalls the servant of Isaiah 53, who “bore the sin of many” (53:12).
vv: Jesus was walking ahead of them; they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid.
He goes first, deliberately, towards the city where he will die. The disciples feel the weight of it before they understand it.
Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.
They believe he will be glorified, which is to their credit. Mark’s readers know who will in fact be at his right and his left: two bandits crucified with him (15:27).
The cup that I drink you will drink;
This came true. James was the first of the Twelve to die for Christ, killed with the sword by Herod (Acts 12:2). John too bore witness through long suffering.
For the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many.
Perhaps the key verse of Mark’s Gospel. The whole life of Jesus is service, and his death is its fullest act.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the redemption won by Christ consists in this, that he came to give his life as a ransom for many (CCC 622). It adds that the word “many” is not restrictive: it sets the whole of humanity over against the one Redeemer who gives himself for all (CCC 605). The Church has always read verses 42–45 as the rule for every authority in her. Pope St Gregory the Great called himself “servant of the servants of God”, a title the popes still use. Whoever holds any office, in the parish or in the family, is measured by this Gospel.

qa: To whom was the ransom paid?

Some early writers spoke as if a price were paid to the devil, but the Church has not made that a teaching. The image is not a business transaction. It means that Christ’s self-giving cost him his life, and that by it we are released from sin and death. He gave himself out of love, to the Father, for us.
rite: St Philip Neri (1515–1595), born in Florence, spent his life in Rome and is called the Apostle of Rome. He gathered priests and lay people for prayer, the reading of Scripture and the lives of the saints, music, and works of charity, and from these gatherings came the Congregation of the Oratory. He was a priest of the confessional and of great joy, known for his humour, which kept both himself and others humble. Today’s Gospel fits him well: he sought no honours, and he served everyone who came to him.
study: Where do I, like James and John, want the place of honour? What would serving look like there instead?
Who in my family or parish serves without being noticed? How can I thank them, and learn from them?

lead: Ben Sira begins a great hymn to God the Creator: by his word his works are made, and no one could ever tire of seeing his glory. In the Gospel a blind beggar at Jericho cries out to the Son of David, receives his sight and follows Jesus on the way. Psalm 33 sings that by the word of the Lord the heavens were made. The one who made the light opens the eyes of a man who could not see it.

r.h: Who could ever tire of seeing his glory?
set: With this passage Ben Sira begins the last great part of his book. First he praises God in creation (42:15–43:33), then he praises the famous ancestors of Israel (chapters 44–50). Nature and history together show God’s glory.
Part of this hymn survives in Hebrew in the scroll of Ben Sira found at Masada, the desert fortress by the Dead Sea. It shows that the book was copied and read in Hebrew in the time of Jesus.
str: v. 15: “I will now call to mind the works of the Lord”: by his word they are made.
vv. 16–17: his glory fills his work; even the holy ones cannot recount it all.
vv. 18–21: he searches the abyss and the human heart; he knows past and future; he needs no counsellor.
vv. 22–25: the beauty of his works; all things in pairs; who could tire of his glory?
kw: “By the word of the Lord his works are made” (v. 15). Ben Sira echoes Genesis 1, where God speaks and things come to be, and Psalm 33:6, today’s psalm. Christians hear the Word who was in the beginning with God (John 1:1–3).
The visible splendour of God. His work is “full of his glory” (v. 16), as the seraphim sing in Isaiah 6:3.
All things come in pairs (v. 24): day and night, life and death. Ben Sira had said this before: “they come in pairs, one the opposite of the other” (33:15). Nothing in creation stands alone.
vv: By the word of the Lord his works are made; and all his creatures do his will.
Creation is not an accident and not a battle between gods, as in some ancient stories. It is the work of a single word, and it obeys.
He searches out the abyss and the human heart;
The God of the deep sea is also the God of the inner heart. Nothing is too large or too hidden for him.
Each supplements the virtues of the other. Who could ever tire of seeing his glory?
Every creature has its own good, and each completes the other. The final question invites the reader to look again, and to keep looking with wonder.
ch: The Catechism quotes the Book of Wisdom: “from the greatness and beauty of created things comes a corresponding perception of their Creator” (Wisdom 13:5; CCC 41). It also teaches that God wills the interdependence of creatures: the sun and the moon, the cedar and the little flower, none of them is sufficient to itself, and they exist only in dependence on each other, to complete each other (CCC 340). That is Ben Sira’s verse 25 in the language of the Church. Pope Francis took up the same vision in Laudato Si’ (2015), calling Christians to care for creation as a common home.

r.h: Your faith has made you well
set: Jericho lies near the Jordan, about twenty-five kilometres from Jerusalem, and far below it. Pilgrims going up to the Passover passed through it. This is the last healing in Mark before Jesus enters Jerusalem.

Mark’s central section began with the healing of a blind man at Bethsaida (8:22–26) and now ends with another. Between them Jesus has tried again and again to open the eyes of the disciples to the meaning of the Cross.
str: v. 46: Bartimaeus sits by the roadside.
vv. 47–48: he cries out to the Son of David; many tell him to be quiet; he cries louder.
vv. 49–50: Jesus stops and calls him; he throws off his cloak and comes.
vv. 51–52: “What do you want me to do for you?” He sees and follows Jesus on the way.
kw: The first time in Mark that anyone calls Jesus by this royal title. A blind man sees what many do not: that Jesus is the promised king from David’s line.
An Aramaic form of address, warmer than “rabbi”. Mary Magdalene uses the same word at the tomb (John 20:16).

Bartimaeus sits beside the way at the start and follows Jesus on the way at the end. In Mark the way leads to Jerusalem and the Cross, and the first Christians called their faith “the Way” (Acts 9:2).
vv: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!

From this cry, with the cry of the tax collector (Luke 18:13), the Eastern Churches drew the Jesus Prayer. The Catechism traces it to the cry of the publican and of the blind men begging for light (CCC 2667).
So throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.
For a beggar the cloak may have been nearly all he owned, his covering at night. He leaves it without a second thought. Compare the rich man, who could not leave his possessions (10:22).
What do you want me to do for you?
The same question Jesus asked James and John (10:36). They asked for glory; the blind man asks to see. Only his request is granted at once.
Immediately he regained his sight and followed him on the way.
The healed man becomes a disciple. He follows Jesus up to Jerusalem, into the week of the Passion.
ch: The Church has seen in Bartimaeus a picture of every believer, and of every catechumen. In the early Church baptism was called “enlightenment” (Greek phōtismos), and the newly baptised received a lighted candle. St Augustine, preaching on the blind men of the Gospels, urges his hearers to cry out to Christ by the way they live, even when the crowd around them tells them to be silent (in substance). The cry “have mercy on me” is heard at every Mass in the Kyrie.

rite: St Augustine of Canterbury (died about 604) was the prior of a monastery in Rome when Pope St Gregory the Great sent him with a band of monks to the English. They landed in Kent in 597, and King Ethelbert was baptised. Augustine became the first Archbishop of Canterbury. Like Bartimaeus, he received the light and followed Christ on the way, a long way from home.
study: What would I answer if Jesus asked me today, “What do you want me to do for you?”
What is my “cloak”, the thing I hold on to, that keeps me from springing up and coming to Jesus?

lead: Ben Sira begins his praise of the ancestors: some left a name, others are forgotten, but the godly ones live on in the covenant and in their children. In the Gospel Jesus enters the Temple and looks around, and the next day curses a barren fig tree and drives out the traders. Then he teaches faith that can move mountains and prayer that forgives. Psalm 149 sings that the Lord takes delight in his people, the faithful whose lives bear fruit.

r.h: Their righteous deeds have not been forgotten
set: Chapters 44–50 are the “Praise of the Ancestors”. Ben Sira walks through Israel’s history from Enoch and Noah to Abraham, Moses, David, the prophets, and finally to the high priest Simon son of Onias, whom he had seen serving at the altar (50:1–21). Few passages in the Old Testament offer so long a gallery of the faithful; the Letter to the Hebrews will do something similar in chapter 11.

Our verses are taken from the introduction. Ben Sira first lists many kinds of famous people (vv. 2–8), then admits that others are forgotten (v. 9), and then says what lasts: the godly, whose goodness lives on.
str: v. 1: “Let us now sing the praises of famous men.”
v. 9: those of whom there is no memory.
vv. 10–13: the godly, whose righteous deeds are not forgotten; their descendants stand by the covenant.
kw: The Greek calls them “men of mercy” (v. 10); the Hebrew word behind it is very likely ḥesed, faithful love. They were good not only for themselves; their love was faithful to God and to others.
Their descendants “stand by the covenants” (v. 12). What keeps a family’s goodness alive is not wealth alone but fidelity to God’s covenant.
Some are forgotten by people, but the question in this passage is who is remembered by God. The godly live on in his memory and in the people they formed.
vv: Let us now sing the praises of famous men, our ancestors in their generations.
To praise the ancestors is to praise God who worked through them. Ben Sira’s list will be honest about their faults too.
But of others there is no memory; they have perished as though they had never existed;
A sober verse. Many lives leave no trace in history. Ben Sira does not pretend otherwise.
But these also were godly men, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten;
The goodness of the faithful does not vanish. It is carried on in their children and in God’s memory.
ch: The Church sings these verses on the feasts of saints, especially of holy founders and pastors. For Christians, the memory that matters most is God’s memory, and the communion of saints means that the godly are not simply remembered: they live in Christ and pray for us (CCC 956). The countless saints whose names no history records are honoured together on All Saints’ Day. Ben Sira also reminds parents and teachers that the greatest legacy is a family that keeps the covenant.

r.h: A house of prayer for all the nations
set: Jesus has entered Jerusalem to the crowd’s acclaim (11:1–10). Mark then sets the cleansing of the Temple between the two halves of the fig tree story: the cursing (vv. 12–14) and the withered tree the next morning (vv. 20–21). This “sandwich” is a favourite way for Mark to let two stories explain each other.

The traders sold animals for sacrifice, and the money changers changed coins into the Tyrian silver used for the Temple tax. This trade was not wicked in itself; pilgrims needed it. Many scholars think it was set up in the great outer court, the only part of the Temple where Gentiles could pray.
str: v. 11: Jesus looks around the Temple and goes out to Bethany.
vv. 12–14: the fig tree with leaves and no fruit.
vv. 15–19: the cleansing of the Temple; the authorities seek to destroy him.
vv. 20–26: the withered fig tree; faith, prayer and forgiveness.
kw: The prophets used the fig tree and its fruit as an image of Israel and its faithfulness (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1). The leaves promise fruit, but there is none. The act is a prophetic sign, not an outburst of temper.
Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7, where the Lord promises that foreigners who hold to his covenant will be joyful in his house of prayer. Only Mark keeps the words “for all the nations”.
From Jeremiah 7:11. A den is where robbers hide, not where they rob. Jeremiah warned that people could not sin and then shelter in the Temple as if it would protect them.
vv: he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.
Mark’s remark shows that the story is not about a tree at all. Jesus seeks fruit out of season, as God seeks fruit from his people at every hour.
My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations
Jesus defends the Temple’s true purpose, prayer, and its wide welcome, the nations. He acts as the prophets did, from within Israel, out of love for the house of his Father.
Have faith in God.
The withered tree becomes a lesson on prayer. Faith moves what seems immovable, because it trusts God, not itself.
Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone;
Prayer that moves mountains must also forgive. Verse 26 is printed in some Bibles, but it is missing from the best ancient manuscripts and was probably added from Matthew 6:15.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus venerated the Temple, went up to it for the feasts, and that his zeal for his Father’s house shows his love, not hostility (CCC 583–584). His action is a prophetic sign of the new Temple, his own body (John 2:21). It must never be read as a rejection of the Jewish people. The Catechism also quotes verse 24 when it speaks of the boldness of a child’s prayer (CCC 2610), and teaches that God’s mercy cannot reach a heart that refuses to forgive (CCC 2840).

qa: Why did Jesus curse a tree for having no figs when it was not the season?

Because the act is a sign, like the signs of the prophets, who broke jars or wore yokes to make a point. Mark frames the Temple scene with it to show what Jesus seeks: not leaves, the outward show of worship, but fruit, a life of prayer, faith and forgiveness. It is a warning to every believer and every community, the Church included.
study: If Jesus came looking for fruit in my life today, what would he find among the leaves?
Is there someone I need to forgive before I can pray with an open heart? What first step can I take?

lead: At the end of his book Ben Sira tells how he sought wisdom from his youth, in prayer before the Temple, and found her. In the Gospel the leaders of the Temple ask Jesus where his authority comes from, and he answers with a question about John the Baptist. Psalm 19 sings that the precepts of the Lord give joy to the heart. The one who seeks wisdom with a pure heart finds her; the one who will not commit himself cannot see the authority standing before him.

r.h: I sought wisdom openly in my prayer
set: Chapter 51 is an appendix to the book: a thanksgiving (vv. 1–12) and a poem about the search for wisdom (vv. 13–30). In Hebrew the poem is an acrostic, each line beginning with the next letter of the alphabet. A Hebrew form of it was found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, in the great Psalms Scroll from the eleventh cave at Qumran.
Here the teacher speaks of himself. After a whole book of advice, he tells his students how he himself came to wisdom: young, praying, persevering.
str: v. 12: thanksgiving for rescue.
vv. 13–14: while still young he prayed for wisdom before the Temple.
vv. 15–17: his heart delighted in her; he made progress and gave glory to God.
vv. 18–20: he resolved to live by her, strove for her, and found her in purity.
kw: In Ben Sira, wisdom is the gift of God that comes to dwell in Israel (24:8) and is found in the Law. She is spoken of as a woman to be loved and sought, not as a set of rules.
Wisdom is not won by study alone. Ben Sira asked for her in prayer before the Temple (vv. 13–14). Solomon too received wisdom by asking (1 Kings 3:9).
“In purity I found her” (v. 20). A clean heart sees clearly. Jesus says the same: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8).
vv: While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.
Ben Sira had travelled (34:12), which in his day was part of a wise man’s education. But the search began earlier, in youth and in prayer.
From the first blossom to the ripening grape my heart delighted in her;
An image of growth over a season. Wisdom is not gained in a day but ripens slowly.
I directed my soul to her, and in purity I found her.
Seeking and finding belong together, as Jesus promises: “search, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7).
ch: The Church sees the fullness of wisdom in Christ, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). The search Ben Sira describes is the search of every young person who prays and asks God how to live. The Catechism teaches that parents have the first responsibility for the education of their children (CCC 2223), and the Church asks pastors and teachers to help them lead the young to prayer and the Word of God. Ben Sira’s story is a quiet encouragement: start young, pray, keep going.

r.h: By what authority?
set: The day after the cleansing of the Temple, Jesus is walking in its courts. The chief priests, the scribes and the elders come to him. These three groups formed the Sanhedrin, the high council, and they are the same three groups named in Jesus’ first prediction of his passion (8:31). The question is natural: who gave this Galilean teacher the right to act in the Temple?
This is the first of a series of debates in the Temple (11:27–12:37). Mark presents particular leaders, not the people, many of whom were “spellbound by his teaching” (11:18).
str: vv. 27–28: the question about authority.
vv. 29–30: Jesus’ counter-question about the baptism of John.
vv. 31–32: the leaders reason among themselves.
v. 33: “We do not know”; Jesus will not tell them either.
kw: Not only power, but the right to act. From the start the crowds noticed that Jesus taught with authority, not as the scribes (1:22, 27).
John called Israel to repentance and pointed to the one coming after him (1:7–8). If his baptism was from heaven, then so is the authority of the one he announced.
A reverent way of saying “from God”, as Jews often did out of respect for the divine name, as in Matthew’s “kingdom of heaven”.
vv: By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority to do them?
The answer is hidden in the question. Jesus’ authority comes from the Father who sent him, but they must be willing to see it.
Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin? Answer me.
Teachers of the time often answered a question with a question. Jesus is not evading; he is showing that the answer depends on whether they accepted John.
So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.”
Their answer is not ignorance but refusal. Those who will not commit themselves to the truth they already know cannot receive more.
ch: The Church confesses that Jesus’ authority is that of the Son, sent by the Father: he did not teach as one interpretation among others, but with the authority of the Son (CCC 581). Before Pilate and before the council he will not prove it by force. The scene also teaches honesty in faith: we cannot ask God for new light while refusing the light we have. The Second Vatican Council teaches that all are bound to seek the truth, especially about God and his Church, and to embrace it when they find it (Dignitatis Humanae 1).

rite: St Paul VI (1897–1978), Giovanni Battista Montini, was pope from 1963 to 1978. He guided the Second Vatican Council to its close and put its reforms into practice, including the renewed Roman Missal of 1970. He wrote Humanae Vitae (1968) and Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975), on evangelisation. In December 1964 he came to Bombay for the International Eucharistic Congress, the first pope to visit India. He was canonised in 2018. His memorial falls on 29 May, the day of his priestly ordination in 1920. Like Ben Sira, he sought wisdom all his life, and he used authority as service.
study: When did I first begin to seek God seriously? What helped me then, and what helps me now?
Is there a truth I already know but avoid, saying “I do not know”?

lead: On the Solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ the three readings of Year B are held together by one phrase: “the blood of the covenant”. At Sinai Moses reads the book of the covenant, the people promise to obey, and he sprinkles them with the blood of the sacrifice. The Letter to the Hebrews says that Christ, the high priest, has entered the true sanctuary with his own blood and become the mediator of a new covenant. In the Gospel, at the Passover meal, Jesus takes the cup and says, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.”

Psalm 116, one of the psalms sung at the Passover meal, gives the response: “I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord.” Before the Gospel the Church may sing the sequence Lauda Sion, written by St Thomas Aquinas, which teaches in verse what the Church believes about this sacrament. In India the Latin Church keeps the solemnity on this Sunday, and where possible a procession with the Blessed Sacrament follows the Mass.

r.h: The blood of the covenant
set: At Mount Sinai God has spoken the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20) and the laws that follow, which scholars call the “Book of the Covenant” (20:22–23:33). Now the covenant is solemnly sealed. Moses goes between God and the people: he tells them the words of the Lord, writes them down, and then performs a rite that binds both sides together.

Background. In the ancient world, covenants between peoples or between a king and his subjects were often sealed with a sacrifice and a shared meal. Blood was the sign of life (Leviticus 17:11). In this rite the same blood touches both the altar, which stands for God, and the people. Just after our passage Moses and the elders go up the mountain, see the God of Israel, and eat and drink in his presence (24:9–11).
str: v. 3: Moses tells the people the words of the Lord; they answer with one voice.
v. 4a: Moses writes down the words.
vv. 4b–5: the altar and the twelve pillars; burnt offerings and offerings of well-being.
v. 6: half the blood dashed against the altar.
v. 7: the book of the covenant read; the people promise to obey.
v. 8: the rest of the blood dashed on the people: “See the blood of the covenant”.
¶ The structure is a double promise. The people say twice that they will do all the Lord has spoken (vv. 3, 7). Between the two promises stand the word written and the sacrifice offered.
kw: A solemn bond of loyalty, not only a contract. God binds himself to Israel and Israel to God: “I will be your God, and you shall be my people” (compare Leviticus 26:12).
For Israel the life is in the blood (Leviticus 17:11), and so blood belongs to God. Sprinkled on altar and people, it makes them in a sense one family, bound by one life.
we will do, and we will be obedient

Literally “we will do and we will hear” (v. 7). Jewish tradition has long admired that the people promised to do before they heard all. The word šāmaʿ, to hear, also means to obey, as in the great prayer “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4).
vv: All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do.
The covenant begins with God’s word and the people’s answer. Worship without obedience would be empty.
set up twelve pillars, corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel.
The whole people stands around the altar. Jesus will choose twelve apostles, and at the Last Supper the Twelve will be at table with him.
Then he took the book of the covenant, and read it in the hearing of the people;
The Word is proclaimed before the blood is sprinkled. The Mass has the same order: the Liturgy of the Word, then the Liturgy of the Eucharist.
See the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you in accordance with all these words.
These are almost the words Jesus will say over the cup (Mark 14:24). The Letter to the Hebrews quotes this verse when it explains the new covenant (Hebrews 9:20).
ch: The Church reads Sinai in the light of the Last Supper. The Catechism teaches that the Eucharist is the memorial of Christ’s Passover, and that in it the sacrifice Christ offered once for all on the Cross remains ever present (CCC 1364). The old covenant was sealed with the blood of animals; the new covenant with the blood of the Son. God’s covenant with Israel has not been revoked (Romans 11:29; CCC 121). The new covenant does not cancel the call of Israel; it brings God’s promises to their fullness in Christ for all peoples.

r.h: How much more the blood of Christ
set: The Letter to the Hebrews is a long sermon, written for Christians who were tired and tempted to fall back. It has no named author. The Church long linked it with St Paul, and it belongs to the Pauline tradition, but most scholars today think it was written by another teacher, and its date is uncertain. It shows Christ as the high priest of the new covenant.

Background. Chapters 8–10 compare Christ with the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). On that one day each year the high priest entered the Holy of Holies, the inner room of the Temple, with the blood of a bull and a goat, to make atonement for himself and the people. Hebrews says that Christ has done this in reality, once for all, in the true sanctuary of heaven. The “ashes of a heifer” recall another rite of cleansing (Numbers 19).
str: vv. 11–12: Christ enters the true sanctuary once for all, with his own blood, and obtains eternal redemption.
vv. 13–14: if animal blood cleansed the flesh, how much more will Christ’s blood cleanse the conscience.
v. 15: he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the eternal inheritance.
kw: A key word of the letter (7:27; 9:12; 10:10). Christ’s sacrifice does not need to be repeated. Every Mass makes present this one sacrifice; it does not add another.
Release by a price, the same family of words as the “ransom” of Mark 10:45. Christ obtains an eternal redemption, not one that has to be renewed each year.
One who stands between two parties to make peace. Moses stood between God and the people at Sinai; Christ is mediator of the new covenant (8:6; 9:15), the one promised in Jeremiah 31:31.
vv: he entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood,
The priest and the victim are the same. Christ does not offer something outside himself; he offers himself.
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God,
The whole Trinity is at work: the Son offers himself to the Father through the Spirit. “Without blemish” recalls the lambs of the Passover and the sacrifices, which had to be perfect.
purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!
The old rites cleansed the body. Christ’s blood reaches the conscience, the inner heart, and sets it to worship. “Dead works” are deeds that lead to death, sinful works.
For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant,
The letter quotes Jeremiah 31 at length just before (8:8–12). The new covenant is written on the heart.
ch: The Council of Trent taught that the Mass is a true sacrifice, the same sacrifice as the Cross, offered now in an unbloody manner (Session 22). The Catechism says that the sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice: only the manner of offering is different (CCC 1367). That is why Hebrews’ “once for all” is not against the Mass. The Mass is the one sacrifice made present, so that each generation may share in it. The Catechism also calls Christ the “high priest of the good things to come” in the heavenly liturgy (CCC 662).

r.h: This is my body, this is my blood
set: It is the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lambs were sacrificed in the Temple in the afternoon and eaten at night in houses in Jerusalem. The Passover meal remembered the night when God brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 12). Families ate the lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, drank cups of wine, retold the story and sang psalms of praise.
The Lectionary leaves out vv. 17–21, where Jesus foretells his betrayal by one of the Twelve. Even so the shadow is there: the meal is the evening before his death.
str: vv. 12–16: the preparation: two disciples, a man carrying a jar of water, the large room upstairs.
v. 22: the bread: “Take; this is my body.”
vv. 23–24: the cup: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.”
v. 25: “I will never again drink of the fruit of the vine until that day…”
v. 26: they sing the hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives.
kw: Over the bread Jesus blesses (v. 22); over the cup he gives thanks (v. 23). Both words describe the Jewish blessings said at meals. From eucharistia, thanksgiving, comes the name Eucharist.
In biblical thought the body is the whole person in his presence and action. “This is my body” means: this is I myself, given for you.

The words echo Exodus 24:8, today’s first reading. Paul and Luke give the form “the new covenant in my blood” (1 Corinthians 11:25; Luke 22:20), recalling Jeremiah 31:31. The blood “poured out for many” recalls the servant of Isaiah 53.
vv: a man carrying a jar of water will meet you; follow him,
Carrying water was usually women’s work, so such a man would be easy to see. Mark shows that Jesus knows and arranges what will happen; he goes to his Passion willingly.
Take; this is my body.
Jesus does not say “this is like my body” or “this stands for my body”. The Church has always taken his words as they stand.
This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
“Poured out” is the language of sacrifice, of blood poured at the altar. Jesus speaks of his death the next day as the sacrifice that seals the new covenant.
When they had sung the hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

Most commentators think this was the second part of the Hallel, Psalms 113–118, sung at the end of the Passover meal. Today’s Psalm 116 belongs to it. Jesus went out to Gethsemane with these psalms on his lips.
ch: The Church believes that in the Eucharist the body and blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ, and therefore the whole Christ, is truly, really and substantially contained (CCC 1374, quoting the Council of Trent). The Council of Trent called the change of the whole substance of bread and wine into the substance of his body and blood transubstantiation (CCC 1376). The Catechism quotes St John Chrysostom: it is not man who makes the gifts become the body and blood of Christ, but Christ himself, who was crucified for us; and St Ambrose: the word of Christ, which could make from nothing what did not exist, can change things that exist into what they were not (CCC 1375, in substance).

The Second Vatican Council calls the Eucharist the source and summit of the whole Christian life (Lumen Gentium 11; CCC 1324). St Augustine told the newly baptised, as they came to receive the body of Christ: be what you see, and receive what you are (in substance, Sermon 272).

qa: Is the bread at Mass a symbol of Christ’s body?

It is a sign, but not only a sign. The Church teaches that after the consecration what looks like bread and wine is truly the body and blood of Christ, his whole living person (CCC 1374, 1376). This is why we kneel, genuflect before the tabernacle, and fast for an hour before Communion. It is a mystery of faith, not something the senses can prove; as Lauda Sion sings, what you do not understand, a lively faith confirms.
If I receive only the host, do I receive the whole Christ?

Yes. The Catechism teaches that Christ is present whole and entire in each of the species, so that Communion under the species of bread alone makes it possible to receive all the fruit of grace of the Eucharist (CCC 1377, 1390). Communion under both kinds is a fuller sign, and the Church allows it on many occasions, but nothing is lacking to those who receive the host.
Why does the Mass say “for many” and not “for all”?

Because those are the words of Jesus in Mark and Matthew, and the Church keeps them. They do not mean that Christ died only for some. The Catechism explains that “many” is not restrictive: it sets the whole of humanity over against the one person of the Redeemer who gives himself for all (CCC 605). Christ died for all; the many are those who receive what he offers.
rite: The feast of Corpus Christi began in the thirteenth century at Liège, in present-day Belgium, inspired by the visions of St Juliana of Cornillon. Pope Urban IV extended it to the whole Church in 1264, and St Thomas Aquinas wrote the texts for its Mass and Office, including Lauda Sion and the hymn Pange lingua, whose last verses, Tantum ergo, are sung at Benediction. In India the solemnity is kept on Sunday, so that the faithful can take part, and in many parishes the Mass is followed by a procession with the Blessed Sacrament through the streets, ending with Benediction. The Church in India also remembers that Pope St Paul VI came to Bombay in 1964 for the International Eucharistic Congress.
study: The people at Sinai said, “we will do, and we will be obedient”. What does my “Amen” at Communion promise?
How do I show, by my body and my manner, that I believe Christ is truly present: in church, before the tabernacle, at Communion?
Hebrews says Christ’s blood cleanses our conscience “to worship the living God”. Is there something on my conscience I should bring to the sacrament of reconciliation?
Jesus’ body was “given” and his blood “poured out”. How can my family become, like the Eucharist, a life given for others?

lead: The month of May closes with the feast of the Visitation. Zephaniah calls Daughter Zion to sing, because the King of Israel, the Lord, is in her midst. In the Gospel Mary, who now carries that Lord within her, goes in haste to Elizabeth. The child in Elizabeth’s womb leaps for joy, and Mary sings the Magnificat.

The responsorial canticle from Isaiah 12 repeats the theme: “Great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.” Instead of Zephaniah, the Mass may use Romans 12:9–16, Paul’s call to sincere love and to rejoicing with those who rejoice: the charity Mary shows in going to serve her kinswoman. The feast replaces the readings of Monday of the Ninth Week in Ordinary Time.

r.h: The Lord is in your midst
set: Zephaniah prophesied in Judah “in the days of King Josiah” (1:1), in the seventh century before Christ, probably before Josiah’s reform. Most of his book is a stern warning about the “day of the Lord” against the pride and idolatry of Jerusalem and the nations. But the book ends with a promise: a humble and lowly remnant will seek refuge in the Lord (3:12), and the Lord will rejoice over his people.
Our passage is that final song of joy. The mood changes completely: from judgment to celebration, from fear to the presence of God.
str: v. 14: the call to joy: sing, shout, rejoice, O daughter Zion.
v. 15: the reason: the Lord has taken away the judgments; the King of Israel is in your midst.
v. 16: do not fear, O Zion.
vv. 17–18: the Lord, a warrior who gives victory, rejoices over you with singing.
kw: A tender name for Jerusalem and her people, pictured as a young woman. The Church has seen in Mary the Daughter of Zion in person (Lumen Gentium 55).
Used twice (vv. 15, 17). The same Hebrew word can mean “within you”. Christian readers have heard in it a hint of Mary, in whose womb the Lord came to dwell.

The first of four cries of joy in v. 14. The Greek translation begins with chaire, “rejoice”, the same word with which the angel greets Mary in Luke 1:28; many commentators hear an echo of Zephaniah there.
vv: Sing aloud, O daughter Zion; shout, O Israel!
The prophet who warned of the day of wrath ends with a song. God’s last word is not judgment but joy.
The king of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst; you shall fear disaster no more.
The reason for joy is not a change of circumstances but a presence. God himself is with his people.
he will rejoice over you with gladness, he will renew you in his love; he will exult over you with loud singing
Not only the people rejoice in God; God rejoices over his people. He sings over them like a bridegroom or a mother.
ch: The Church reads this song on the feast of the Visitation because it is fulfilled in Mary. The Second Vatican Council calls her the exalted Daughter of Zion, in whom, after the long waiting, the times are fulfilled (Lumen Gentium 55). The Catechism calls her the Ark of the Covenant, the place where the glory of the Lord dwells: she is the dwelling of God among men (CCC 2676). The Lord who was in the midst of Zion is now in the midst of Mary, and she carries him into a house in the hill country.

r.h: The mother of my Lord comes to me
set: The angel Gabriel has told Mary that she will conceive the Son of the Most High, and has given her a sign: her kinswoman Elizabeth, old and called barren, is in her sixth month (1:36). Mary sets out at once. The hill country of Judea lay some days’ walk south of Nazareth. An ancient tradition places Zechariah’s home at Ein Karem, near Jerusalem.

Background. Luke tells the story with echoes of David bringing the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). David asked, “How can the ark of the Lord come into my care?” (6:9); he danced before the Lord; and the ark stayed in the house of Obed-edom three months (6:11). Elizabeth asks a similar question, John leaps for joy, and Mary stays about three months. Many commentators see in this a picture of Mary as the new Ark, carrying the Lord himself.
str: vv. 39–40: Mary goes in haste to the house of Zechariah and greets Elizabeth.
